title: [tunnel-infra] TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN is not in the prod secret bundle — deploy blocker
description:
Verified read-only against AWS on 2026-09-19 during the tunnel/integration merge.

The prod bundle arn:aws:secretsmanager:us-east-2:033937118837:secret:debuggai-api-prod/creds-Sv64xe holds 42 keys. TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN is NOT one of them. All 39 entries of required_secrets ARE present, so nothing is broken today — but the tunnel work names a key that does not exist.

What breaks, in order, on the first deploy after this lands:
1. deploy/prod/rc.yml's tunnel service has env_from_secret keys: [TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN], and deploy/prod/task-secrets.json gives the debuggai-api-tunnel family secrets: [TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN]. ECS resolves bundle JSON keys at task launch; a missing key is ResourceInitializationError, not a warning. The tunnel task never starts.
2. The integration branch additionally gives the django family extra_secrets: [TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN] (django is the verifier; settings.TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN empty = fail closed = every verify 401s). With the key missing, the NEW django task def cannot start either — that is a django outage, not just a tunnel one.

Fix before landing: add TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN to vault env 'debuggai-api-prod'. Vault is the source of truth — .github/workflows/deploy.yml step 'Refresh vault secrets -> Secrets Manager bundle' does put-secret-value with the WHOLE vault JSON, so a key added directly in Secrets Manager is erased on the next deploy. That step runs before reconcile_task_secrets.py, so once vault has it the deploy self-heals.

The same value must be set as TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN for the tunnel server and read by django's TunnelServiceTokenAuthentication.
notes:
CORRECTION (same session, after checking live ECS): the line above saying a missing key is
"a django outage" OVERSTATES it. The django and nginx services run minimumHealthyPercent 100
with deploymentCircuitBreaker {enable: true, rollback: true}, so the old django tasks keep
serving and ECS rolls the deployment back. The accurate statement is: FAILED DEPLOY with
automatic rollback, not an outage. Nothing ships until vault has the key, but prod keeps
running on the current revision.

Also confirmed, so it is NOT part of this blocker: rc creates the ECR repo for a brand-new
service by itself (remote_compose/services/ecr_service.py get_or_create_repository, called
from the image build service and the ECR deploy step; terraform emits aws_ecr_repository per
service). The absence of a debuggai-api/tunnel repo today is expected and harmless.
close_reason: Resolved 2026-09-19: TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN created in the debuggai-api-prod vault (bundle went 42 -> 43 keys) before the tunnel service deployed. Verified present via simpli exchange.

title: Confirm ngrok account plan supports wildcard endpoints
description: Blocking gate before any code. ngrok's own docs (https://ngrok.com/docs/universal-gateway/domains/) say wildcard endpoints require a paid plan (Pay-as-you-go+); a third-party blog claimed Enterprise-only — conflicting, unverified secondary source. Check the actual debugg.ai ngrok account/dashboard for: (1) current plan tier, (2) whether a wildcard domain can be reserved under ngrok.debugg.ai today without a plan change. Cannot be checked from an agent sandbox — needs real dashboard/account access.
close_reason: Superseded — design no longer depends on ngrok wildcard-domain tunnel binding at all. Confirmed the npm 'ngrok' wrapper spawns the v3 agent (README: 'Version 5 of this project uses ngrok client version 3'), and ngrok's own docs describe v3 wildcard-domain agent endpoints — but whether this specific wrapper's legacy 'hostname' passthrough actually triggers that binding (vs. rejecting a literal '*') was unverified and would have needed a live billed test to settle. Owner decided to skip that risk entirely: redesigned around ONE tunnel + Caddy dynamic single-upstream repoint instead of wildcard Host-header multiplexing. See updated epic description.

title: tunnelRegistry prune orphans LIVE tunnels — they keep billing but become undiscoverable
description:
CORRECTION (2026-07-27): the live evidence originally attached to this bead was WRONG and has been withdrawn. The mechanism is still real in code; the incident was not.

WHAT I GOT WRONG: I read /tmp/debugg-ai-tunnels.json. tunnelRegistry.ts:50 uses join(tmpdir(), ...), and on macOS os.tmpdir() honours $TMPDIR, which under launchd is per-user — here /var/folders/kg/sm6b47f91gg3s12lgtf35ht40000gn/T. The REAL registry contained a healthy :3011 entry (ownerPid 15751, touched minutes earlier) the whole time. There was no orphan. My hand-written /tmp entry sat at a path the code never reads and had no effect; the probe_page success I credited to it was the system working normally. The bogus file has been deleted.

MECHANISM (still real, from code):
- tunnelManager.ts:123-135 constructor prunes entries older than REGISTRY_PRUNE_THRESHOLD_MS (60min, :98). tunnelRegistry.ts:137-157 deletes the map key only — no ngrok reference, no disconnect. Deleting an entry cannot stop a tunnel.
- The singleton is built at module load (:757), so every MCP start sweeps every other process's entries.
- AMPLIFIER: nothing ever re-registers a live tunnel. touchTunnel (:243-249) updates lastAccessedAt only 'if (entry)'; the reuse path (:382-390) returns from the in-process map without touching the registry. So a pruned entry is never restored and the tunnel is permanently invisible while its owner keeps using it.
- IMMORTALITY: the auto-shutoff extension check (:733-747) reads reg.read()[String(port)] and compares lastAccessedAt WITHOUT comparing entry.tunnelId to tunnelInfo.tunnelId. Once a replacement owns the port's entry, the old tunnel extends itself off the replacement's activity, indefinitely. This is what would turn a 55-minute mistake into a multi-day one.

SIGNATURE TO WATCH FOR (the real one): $TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json missing a port that 127.0.0.1:404x/api/tunnels still lists.

RECOMMENDED FIX: reconcile against the local ngrok agent inspector at startup and RE-ADOPT live tunnels into the registry; never have prune shut tunnels down (that costs a 2-billed-hour churn per idle gap > 60min, on exactly the days-long-session pattern the team optimises for). Plus: re-register on touch/reuse when the owner holds the tunnel, and scope the auto-shutoff extension to tunnelId. Verification asymmetry: only a REACHABLE inspector that does not list the tunnel proves death; unreachable is 'unknown' and falls back to today's behaviour.

title: check_app_in_browser: task-specified credentials must beat environment defaults at every login
description:
Client report (env 700b0a57-4f7c-466b-81d8-d61ed6f13572; executions cab2731f, 56e836e0): at a mid-flow login wall the agent auto-filled the environment's default credential (qatest123@example.com) instead of the account the task named, so a working app flow reported 'No active account found with the given credentials'.

Root causes (backend, platform/sentinal):
1. auth_deterministic._resolve_credentials ordered resolved_credential_id -> project default -> inline env, so caller-supplied creds were LAST.
2. browser.setup adopted the environment's default credential whenever resolved_credential_id was empty — including the ephemeral-credential case where EnvironmentResolver deliberately reports None for a brand-new account.
3. browser.setup published resolution.credential.uuid directly instead of resolved_ids, leaking a phantom UUID whose lookup missed and fell through to a default.
4. fill_login_credentials took selectors only and always filled the stored account, so 'sign in as X' mid-flow was unexpressible.

Fixes landed: new node_executors/credential_precedence.py (single precedence authority with provenance), browser.setup guards, fill_login_credentials(email,password), goal/system-prompt identity wording, evidence.logins + evidence.login_error surfacing.

MCP side: loginCredentials[], useEnvironmentCredentials, auth.username/password, logins/loginError/credentialWarning in the response, README + tool-description guidance.

title: Tunnel reuse replays the CREATING call's path: port-keyed cache returns stale publicUrl, so probe/check of '/' silently lands on another session's path
description:
The tunnel cache is keyed by PORT but stores a PATH. Any reuse/borrow of an existing
tunnel returns the path baked in by whichever call CREATED that tunnel, silently
discarding the path the caller actually asked for. The caller is then told, via a
sanitized response, that it landed on the URL it requested. It did not.

## Reproduced on demand (2026-07-14)

probe_page targeting `http://localhost:3011/` (executionId 4d1db35b-7536-4334-a706-36986a793899):

    requested : http://localhost:3011/
    navigated : http://localhost:3011/projects/83fa71e2-ff6d-4cc3-9c19-272b024f08fa/graphs
    error     : TimeoutError: Page.goto ... navigating to ".../projects/83fa71e2-.../graphs"

That path is byte-for-byte the `publicUrl` in the live registry at the time. `/` was never
requested.

## Mechanism (all refs are current @ 3e26441)

1. `utils/urlParser.ts:132-141` — `generateTunnelUrl()` builds the public URL as
   `https://<tunnelId>.<domain>` + `parsed.pathname + parsed.search + parsed.hash`.
   The comment states the intent: "Create the tunneled URL maintaining the path, search,
   and hash". Correct for a one-shot call; wrong the moment the result is CACHED, because
   the path is request-scoped state stored on a tunnel-scoped record.

2. `services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts:540` — `createTunnel()` persists that path-bearing
   string as `TunnelInfo.publicUrl` (field decl `:60`), alongside a SEPARATE, correct,
   path-free `tunnelUrl` (origin only).

3. Every lookup is by port alone and returns the stale `publicUrl` verbatim:
   - `tunnelManager.ts:329-333` in-process reuse — `getTunnelForPort(port)` →
     `return { url: existing.publicUrl, ... }`
   - `tunnelManager.ts:352-377` cross-process BORROW — `registry[String(port)]` →
     `return { url: regEntry.publicUrl, ... }`. Note `:362` stores the caller's new URL as
     `originalUrl` while still returning the OLD `publicUrl` — the discard is explicit.
   - `utils/tunnelContext.ts:56-64` `findExistingTunnel()` →
     `return { ...ctx, targetUrl: existing.publicUrl }` — same discard, third site.
   `extractLocalhostPort()` is the only key. Path/search/hash never participate.

4. `services/ngrok/tunnelRegistry.ts:50` — the registry is a SHARED FILE:
   `join(tmpdir(), 'debugg-ai-tunnels.json')`. It is cross-session and cross-PID, so ONE
   session that first tunnels a port with a path poisons EVERY other session's calls to
   that port, and it survives restarts of the victim session, `.next` wipes, and cache
   clears. Liveness/TTL checks (`isEntryUsable`, bead 3th) gate PID-reuse — they do not
   look at the path.

5. `utils/tunnelContext.ts:110+` — `sanitizeResponse()` rewrites tunnel URLs in the
   response back to the original localhost origin. This is what makes the bug so hard to
   see: the wrong path is reported under the RIGHT origin (`http://localhost:3011/...`),
   so it reads as though the APP redirected you. It masks the tunnel's involvement
   entirely.

## Live registry evidence

`$TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json` at time of repro — note `publicUrl` carries a path while
`tunnelUrl` (the fix material) is clean, and `ownerPid` is a DIFFERENT session:

    "3011": {
      "tunnelId":  "687ba5fa-8dd5-45df-bfa2-32cdc09804f5",
      "publicUrl": "https://687ba5fa-...ngrok.debugg.ai/projects/83fa71e2-.../graphs",
      "tunnelUrl": "https://687ba5fa-...ngrok.debugg.ai",
      "ownerPid":  96730
    },
    "4021": {
      "publicUrl": "https://43714351-...ngrok.debugg.ai/t/draft",
      "tunnelUrl": "https://43714351-...ngrok.debugg.ai",
      "ownerPid":  97277
    }

Both entries are poisoned, with two unrelated paths. This is not an edge case; it is the
steady state of any session that probes a sub-path before probing root.

## Why this burned ~a day and produced FOUR wrong root causes

The symptom is a function of REGISTRY STATE, not of the app, the browser, or the config —
so it is bistable and looks haunted:
- Rock-solid consistent for hours = tunnel alive and being reused/touched.
- "Fixed itself" = something recreated the tunnel from a root-path call.
- "Unreproducible" = the baked path CHANGED (`/test-knowledge-graph` →
  `/projects/83fa71e2-.../graphs`). The bug never went away; it moved.
- Immune to victim-side restarts = the poisoned entry is owned by ANOTHER session's PID.

Disproven along the way (do not revisit): app routing/`returnTo` (the route is real and
renders fine); browser-state reuse (`debugg_ai_mcp-hky0`, closed NOT-A-BUG); a
storage-reset fix (`sentinal-6qz1t`, solved a non-problem, merged anyway); stale dev
server / `.next`; backend reachability and `NEXT_PUBLIC_API_BASE_URL` (a dead-port repro is
clean both locally and remotely); "leaked MCP/ngrok processes" (checked ppid — every proc
had a LIVE `claude` parent; N sessions x 2 configured servers x 3 procs explains the list;
nothing was orphaned).

Prior sighting of the same bug, mis-filed at the time: an environment's stored url was
`https://<id>.ngrok.debugg.ai/reset-password` — a tunnel URL with a stale path baked in.
Same mechanism, different path.

## Fix

The data model already separates the two concepts — `tunnelUrl` (origin, tunnel-scoped) vs
`publicUrl` (origin+path, request-scoped). The bug is only that the request-scoped value is
the one cached and returned. On every reuse/borrow, rebuild the target from the CURRENT
request instead of replaying the old one:

    generateTunnelUrl(ctx.originalUrl, existing.tunnelId)   // origin from tunnel, path from caller

Apply at all three sites: `tunnelManager.ts:333`, `tunnelManager.ts:376`,
`tunnelContext.ts:63`.

Stronger variant worth considering: stop persisting `publicUrl` on `TunnelInfo` and in the
registry at all. Store only `tunnelUrl` + `tunnelId` (tunnel-scoped facts) and derive the
target per request. That makes the bug structurally unrepresentable rather than fixed in
three places where a fourth call site can reintroduce it.

## Tasks

1. RED test first: seed/borrow a tunnel for port 3011 created from
   `http://localhost:3011/foo`, then request `http://localhost:3011/`; assert the returned
   target ends in `/`, not `/foo`. Cover all three sites (in-process reuse, cross-process
   borrow, `findExistingTunnel`) plus search/hash preservation.
2. Apply the fix (prefer removing persisted `publicUrl`; otherwise derive at all 3 sites).
3. Registry hygiene: existing on-disk entries are already poisoned. Either ignore/migrate
   `publicUrl` on read, or bump a registry schema version so stale entries are dropped —
   otherwise the fix ships and users stay broken until `$TMPDIR` clears.
4. Regression-test the cross-session path specifically (two "PIDs", one port, different
   paths) — that is the variant that made this survive restarts.
5. Verify live: `rm $TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json`, probe `:3011/foo`, then probe `:3011/`,
   confirm the second lands on `/`.

Interim workaround for anyone blocked: `rm $TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json`. Band-aid only —
any live session that re-tunnels with a path immediately re-poisons it.

Related: `debugg_ai_mcp-hky0` (closed, wrong cause), `sentinal-6qz1t` (fix for a
non-problem), `react-web-app-4aca`. See sibling review bead for the surrounding audit.
acceptance_criteria: A reuse/borrow of an existing tunnel for a port returns the CALLER's path, never the creating call's path. RED test exists first and covers all 3 sites (tunnelManager reuse :333, cross-process borrow :376, tunnelContext.findExistingTunnel :63) incl. the two-PID/one-port cross-session case. Pre-existing poisoned registry entries in $TMPDIR/debugg-ai-tunnels.json do not survive the upgrade (ignored on read, migrated, or schema-versioned). Live check passes: rm registry, probe :3011/foo, then probe :3011/ -> lands on /.
notes:
FIX COMMITTED (branch fix/zmc9-tunnel-path-retarget, 641c6d3) — UNIT-VERIFIED, live cross-session repro NOT yet run, so leaving OPEN.

Fix: a tunnel is origin-scoped; the path is request-scoped. Added
retargetTunnelUrl(tunnelOrigin, requestedUrl) = reused tunnel's origin (the path-free
tunnelUrl that was already stored) + THIS request's path/search/hash. Wired into all four
reuse sites that previously replayed the creator's publicUrl:
  - services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts in-process reuse (was :352), pending-join (was :368), borrow (was :395)
  - utils/tunnelContext.ts findExistingTunnel (was :63)
The fresh-create site is unchanged — its publicUrl already carries the current caller's path.

Verification done: full suite 852 pass; 2 new findExistingTunnel regression tests go RED without
the source fix (request '/', assert '/' is returned, not the cached deep path) and GREEN with it;
retargetTunnelUrl unit tests cover caller-path retarget, root repro, search+hash, stale-origin
stripping, invalid-input fallback. tsc/lint/build clean.

Verification NOT done (why still open): the live cross-session repro from this bead — poison a port
from session A with a deep path, then confirm session B's request for '/' navigates to '/' rather
than inheriting the deep path. Needs a real tunnel provision. Recommend running it before merge/close.

Note the shared-registry poison root (bead point 4) still stands as designed — the registry is a
shared cross-PID file; this fix stops the poison from producing a WRONG PATH, but the entry is still
shared. Sibling theme: k34o (tunnel-layer audit). Also note ERR_NGROK_3200 on reuse (borrowing a
DEAD tunnel) is a DIFFERENT failure than this stale-PATH bug; that one is caught early now by the
merged z15n pre-flight probe (probeTunnelHealth) but not prevented — prevention = verify tunnel
liveness before borrow, not covered here.
LIVE-VERIFIED against a REAL provisioned ngrok tunnel (2026-07-17). Fix is proven.

Harness: minted a real backend key (prod api.debugg.ai), established a real ngrok tunnel via
ensureTunnel for http://localhost:39119/deep/creator/path (so publicUrl is poisoned with the deep
path), then exercised the ACTUAL fixed reuse path (findExistingTunnel + tunnelManager.getTunnelForPort)
against that live tunnel. Real tunnelId 31719bd1-...; origin https://31719bd1-...ngrok.debugg.ai.

Results (all PASS):
  - setup: stored publicUrl carries the creator deep path  (poison confirmed present)
  - caller '/'            reuse -> https://<origin>/                    (NOT the deep path) ✓ THE FIX
  - caller '/other?x=1'   reuse -> https://<origin>/other?x=1                                ✓
  - caller '/deep/creator/path' reuse -> https://<origin>/deep/creator/path (unchanged when it matches) ✓
Before the fix, all three would have returned the cached deep path (the exact zmc9 bug).

Reachability-via-shell-curl was INCONCLUSIVE (curl exit 28 = timeout, IDENTICAL on both '/' and the
deep path) — the debugg.ai ngrok edge does not serve plain shell curl from this host. This does NOT
bear on the fix: (a) it fails equally for every path, so it is not path-specific; (b) in production the
REMOTE BROWSER reaches these tunnels (that is how the tool works at all), and an ngrok tunnel is
origin-scoped — it forwards EVERY path to the same 127.0.0.1:port; (c) the bug's own original repro
proved the backend browser navigates to whatever targetUrl we hand it — we now hand it the correct one.

Verification ledger:
  - unit: 852 pass; 2 findExistingTunnel regression tests RED without the source fix, GREEN with;
    retargetTunnelUrl units (caller-path, root repro, search+hash, stale-origin strip, invalid fallback).
  - live: reuse of a real poisoned tunnel returns the caller's path, not the creator's (above).
  - tsc/lint/build clean. No leaked servers/tunnels/registry entries after the run.
Commit 641c6d3 on branch fix/zmc9-tunnel-path-retarget. Not yet merged to main.

Still distinct and NOT addressed here: ERR_NGROK_3200 on reuse = borrowing a DEAD tunnel (stale
ENDPOINT, not stale PATH). Caught early now by the merged z15n pre-flight probe, not prevented.
Prevention = verify tunnel liveness before borrow. Sibling k34o (tunnel-layer audit).
MERGED + PUSHED to origin/main (merge 5ac4e0a, reconciled via f1bdeea, commit 641c6d3). Closing: unit-verified (852 tests, 2 regression tests RED without the fix), live-verified against a real ngrok tunnel (reuse of a poisoned tunnel returns the caller's path, not the creator's deep path), tsc/lint/build clean. The stale-PATH-on-reuse bug is fixed at all four reuse sites. NOTE the sibling still open: ERR_NGROK_3200 on reuse = borrowing a DEAD tunnel (stale ENDPOINT, not stale path) — caught early by the merged z15n pre-flight probe but not prevented; prevention (verify tunnel liveness before borrow) is the logical next fix. See k34o (tunnel-layer audit).

title: Partial results on timeout
description:
From the two-system spec for check_app_in_browser. Meta-root-cause: the App Evaluation ('explore & tell me what you see') workload is forced through assertion-based pass/fail termination + a perception layer built for deterministic E2E tests. The MCP is a THIN user surface: define WHAT to test + HOW to drive the agent, then relay the result honestly — relay, never invent; complexity belongs server-side. Keep mature plumbing (tunnels/retries/polling/reachability) as-is. Tests are Jest (jest.config.js).

services/workflows.ts:272 THROWS on the 10-min poll timeout, discarding any captured screenshot/trace (result-shaping at :435+ is bypassed). Instead shape + return the last observed execution: partial actionTrace + screenshot + outcome:'timeout'. Always attach the last screenshot on non-success.

CROSS-EPIC DEP: depends on the backend contract item sentinal-k8x1f.4 (evidence on every terminal state).
design: Files: services/workflows.ts:272 (throws on poll timeout), :435+ (result-shaping bypassed). Shape last observed execution into partial trace + screenshot + outcome:timeout.
acceptance_criteria: TDD (Jest): a simulated poll-timeout returns a shaped result (partial trace + screenshot + outcome:timeout), not a bare thrown error.

title: Relay the verdict faithfully
description:
From the two-system spec for check_app_in_browser. Meta-root-cause: the App Evaluation ('explore & tell me what you see') workload is forced through assertion-based pass/fail termination + a perception layer built for deterministic E2E tests. The MCP is a THIN user surface: define WHAT to test + HOW to drive the agent, then relay the result honestly — relay, never invent; complexity belongs server-side. Keep mature plumbing (tunnels/retries/polling/reachability) as-is. Tests are Jest (jest.config.js).

Stop fabricating: testPageChangesHandler.ts:438 falls outcome->raw status; :499 defaults success:false on thin state; :524-534 synthesizes assertion-mismatch. Consume the backend's EXPLICIT verdict; map unknown/error/timeout/null -> inconclusive (NOT failure); source stepsBudget from the response, not the 25 constant (tools/testPageChanges.ts:17).

CROSS-EPIC DEP: depends on the backend contract items sentinal-k8x1f.2 (explicit verdict) and sentinal-k8x1f.3 (per-run budget in the response).
design: Files: handlers/testPageChangesHandler.ts:438 (outcome->raw status), :499 (success:false default), :524-534 (synthesized assertion-mismatch); tools/testPageChanges.ts:17 (25 constant). Verdict enum from backend: pass|fail|inconclusive|error|timeout.
acceptance_criteria: TDD (Jest): a backend inconclusive/unknown surfaces as inconclusive; no fabricated assertion-mismatch on thin state; reported budget matches the backend.
close_reason: Relay verdict faithfully via verdictAdapter; no fabrication; budget from response. PR #15.

description:

services/workflows.ts:154 resolves the workflow by keyword name-substring and IGNORES its name arg; handlers/testPageChangesHandler.ts:42 hardcodes a DIFFERENT literal 'app evaluation' used as the cache key (:250). title: Thin the MCP: consume the contract, relay honestly, invent nothing
description: PRD B of the two-system browser-verification spec for check_app_in_browser. Meta-root-cause: the App Evaluation ('explore & tell me what you see') workload is forced through assertion-based pass/fail termination + a perception layer built for deterministic E2E tests. The MCP is a THIN user surface for defining WHAT to test and HOW to drive the agent, then relaying the result honestly — relay, never invent; complexity belongs server-side. Keep the mature plumbing (tunnels/retries/polling/reachability) as-is. Tests are Jest (jest.config.js). Cross-epic deps to the backend epic (sentinal) are encoded as text in each child description since bd cannot link across workspaces.
design: Two-system spec: MCP (PRD B) is a thin relay over the backend (Spec A, repo sentinal, epic sentinal-k8x1f). Consume the backend explicit-verdict + evidence contract; do not fabricate outcomes.

title: [surface] P4 · Implementation (TDD)
description:

title: [epic] Migrate local-dev ngrok tunnels (webhook ingress) off ngrok
description:
The product tunnel is fully migrated, but LOCAL DEV still depends on ngrok in two places. This BLOCKS closing the ngrok account.

WHAT STILL USES NGROK
1. sentinal/local.yml 'ngrok' service: binds the reserved domain debuggai-backend.ngrok.app -> sentinal_django:8002. Carries GitHub webhooks (the debugg-ai-test GitHub App has this URL registered) and SDK ingest (DEBUGG_AI_INGEST_URL defaults to it). Needs NGROK_AUTHTOKEN in backend/.envs/.local/.ngrok. Documented in platform README.md:207 and CLAUDE.md:80; agent boxes deliberately exclude it (scripts/agent-box-up.sh:87,175) because a reserved domain can only be bound once.
2. react-web-app/dev-utils/ngrok-config.yml: binds 1234.ngrok.debugg.ai -> localhost:3011 for VS Code extension dev. Note this is on ngrok.debugg.ai, whose DNS is also slated for deletion.

WHY THIS IS NOT THE SAME PROBLEM WE JUST SOLVED
The product tunnel carries OUR OWN browsers (inside our VPC) to a developer's localhost. This carries the PUBLIC INTERNET (GitHub's webhook senders) to a developer's localhost. Three gaps follow:
- Reachability: tunnel.debugg.ai resolves ONLY inside the VPC by design. GitHub cannot reach it. Needs the public path first (bead xkoh.8).
- Stable hostname: a webhook URL is registered once with GitHub and must not change. Our tunnel ids are a fresh uuid per tunnel; this needs named/reserved tunnels, a concept the server does not have.
- Client shape: our client is TypeScript inside the MCP npm package. Local dev needs something a docker-compose service can run and keep alive, i.e. a small standalone CLI or container image.
Single-holder semantics already match: the server replaces an existing connection when a new verified one arrives for the same tunnel id, which is the same 'only one place can hold it' rule the ngrok reserved domain has.

SEQUENCING (the important part)
Do NOT close the ngrok account or delete *.ngrok.debugg.ai DNS until this lands, or local dev webhooks and the VS Code dev tunnel break for everyone. That supersedes the earlier 'safe to close the account' guidance, which only considered the product tunnel.

Scope as its own test-first arc once xkoh.8 (public tunnel URLs) is decided.
notes:
SCOPE REVISED 2026-09-25 after surveying what actually depends on ngrok. The original scoping assumed this needed public wildcard tunnels (xkoh.8). It probably does not, and the cheaper design also keeps the security posture we deliberately chose.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY LIVE (all local-dev; production is clean):
- sentinal/local.yml ngrok container -> GitHub webhooks to a dev's local django. THE only thing that genuinely needs to be reachable from the public internet.
- config/settings/local.py:351-352 API_BASE_URL / APP_BASE_URL default to the ngrok domain.
- projects/models.py:805-809 get_ingest_url() returns the ngrok URL when settings.DEBUG, and api.debugg.ai otherwise — so PROD IS SAFE, this is a dev-only branch. Same for the base.py:2820 default.
- react-web-app/dev-utils/ngrok-config.yml (1234.ngrok.debugg.ai -> Next.js dev on 3011) is referenced by NOTHING in either repo. Almost certainly stale — confirm, then just delete it.

THE KEY OBSERVATION: the GitHub receiver is config/urls.py:49, api/v1/webhooks/github/ — a single path, a plain function view, one POST with a body. No browser, no root-absolute assets, no HMR. Path-prefix routing is therefore completely safe here, which is what killed the Feb 2026 multiplexer for BROWSER traffic (a browser re-requests /_next/... against the origin and loses the prefix; a webhook never makes a second request).

CHEAPER DESIGN TO EVALUATE FIRST: serve dev webhooks on the ALREADY-PUBLIC api.debugg.ai under a path, e.g. https://api.debugg.ai/dev-webhooks/<name>/, routed to the tunnel server and forwarded down that dev's named tunnel to their local api/v1/webhooks/github/. Then:
- no new public DNS, no wildcard public cert, no xkoh.8 dependency;
- *.tunnel.debugg.ai STAYS VPC-private, so the security question flagged on arc 1 (a named public hostname is neither unguessable nor unreachable) largely goes away — the relay can require a shared secret and can only ever forward to the one webhook path;
- still needs stable/named tunnels (so the registered URL does not change) and the standalone dev client, i.e. arcs 17.1 and 17.2 survive, but 17.1 loses its public-exposure half.
The other dev uses need no tunnel at all: point API_BASE_URL/APP_BASE_URL and the DEBUG ingest URL at localhost.

Revisit arc 17.1's requirements phase with this before building. If the relay design holds, this epic is substantially smaller than the 29 beads first scoped.

title: [tunnel-infra] rolling peak no longer fits the 2-instance prod fleet after nginx resize + tunnel service
description:
Found during the tunnel/integration merge (2026-09-19), by recomputing the ec2_capacity
arithmetic that deploy/prod/rc.yml's own comments carry, against LIVE ECS numbers
(read-only describe-container-instances, nothing mutated).

The infra branch adds 1792 MiB of steady reservation to a fleet the comments describe as
already "tight and deliberate": the new tunnel service (1024 MiB) plus nginx going
256 -> 1024 MiB. The nginx comment accounts for its own +768 MiB ("against ~6 GiB spare
... so it fits"), but nothing recomputed the ROLLING PEAK, and nothing counted the tunnel
service's own burst.

Computed from rc.yml (max% = 200 unless the service declares deployment.maximum_percent;
celery-worker and celery-browser are 50/100 and roll in place, so they contribute nothing):

  steady            27136 MiB  (26.50 GiB)   was 25344 MiB / 24.75 GiB
  rolling burst     +5632 MiB  ( 5.50 GiB)   was +3328 MiB / 3.25 GiB
  peak              32768 MiB  (32.00 GiB)   was 28672 MiB / 28.00 GiB
  registered LIVE   31286 MiB  (30.55 GiB)   2 x m5.xlarge, ec2_capacity max: 2

  SHORTFALL AT PEAK = 1482 MiB.

rc.yml's own comment says "The rolling peak after the 50/100 celery change is 28.00 GiB =
91%, which fits without a third box." After this branch it is 32.00 GiB = 105%. It does not
fit.

Worse, the free memory is FRAGMENTED, and ECS places a task on one instance:

  i-03f0df274280b427c  4 tasks  9728/15559 MiB used, 5831 MiB free
  i-099350d4789365bf3  7 tasks 15616/15727 MiB used,  111 MiB free
  fleet free: 5942 MiB, but 98% of it is on ONE box.

Placing the tunnel task (1024 MiB) is fine. The roll is not: only ~4.8 GiB of placeable
room remains on a single instance against a 5.5 GiB burst, and ec2_capacity max: 2 means
ECS managed scaling CANNOT add a third instance — max is described in rc.yml as "the ONLY
control here", because desired is owned by target-tracking. So the failure mode is tasks
stuck in PENDING until old ones drain, i.e. exactly platform-6bu.

Options for the owner (not chosen here, nothing changed):
  a) raise ec2_capacity max to 3 for the deploy that introduces the tunnel service;
  b) give tunnel (and/or nginx) deployment: {minimum_healthy_percent: 50, maximum_percent: 100}
     so they roll in place like the celery pools — reasonable for tunnel at replicas: 1
     only if a brief tunnel outage is acceptable, and NOT reasonable for nginx;
  c) start tunnel smaller than 1024 MiB (it is a byte-pipe, and the 512/1024 in rc.yml is
     explicitly "a starting point to watch, not a measurement");
  d) accept a slower roll.

This does not block correctness of the merge; it blocks a clean first deploy.
notes: RESOLVED in the integration branch (owner chose option b, 2026-09-19): tunnel 1024->512 AND nginx 1024->512. Option b on the tunnel alone saved 1024 MiB at peak against a 1482 MiB shortfall, so it was still 458 MiB short; trimming the nginx bump the same way closes it. New arithmetic, same method as the original: steady 26112 MiB (25.50 GiB), burst +4608 MiB (4.50 GiB), peak 30720 MiB (30.00 GiB) vs 31286 MiB registered = 566 MiB headroom, and the 4.50 GiB burst fits the 5831 MiB free on the roomier instance. rc.yml's ec2_capacity comment was updated with these numbers so the next person does not inherit a stale claim. Not closing until the first roll confirms placement.
close_reason: Resolved 2026-09-19: tunnel and nginx sized at 512 MiB each (not 1024), then redis 512->256 and celery-flower 1024->512 from 7d of measured AWS/ECS MemoryUtilization. Rolling peak 28.50 GiB vs 30.55 registered, ~2.1 GiB headroom. Deployed; all services healthy 5 days later. NOTE: celery-browser peaks at 99.7% of its reservation and was deliberately left alone.

title: [tunnel-mcp-client] debuggTransport dropped frames that arrived in the handshake tick
description:
Found by the tunnel SERVER arc's integration tests, after this arc's 4.1 closed.

THE BUG
debuggTransport built its TunnelSession inside the websocket's 'open' handler, and attached the session's 'stream' listener later still, in adopt() — which runs a microtask after connect() resolves. The server registers a tunnel the instant the handshake completes and may send OPEN in that same tick. Those frames were parsed into a session nobody was listening to and silently dropped: the browser request hung, with no error on either side.

WHY IT MATTERED MORE THAN IT LOOKS
Invisible to every unit test that awaits connect() before driving frames, which is all of them. It lands exactly in the reconnect gap — a deploy (GOAWAY) or a dropped socket is precisely what puts requests in the window between handshake completion and client setup — so in production it would have read as a rare, unexplainable hang rather than a clean failure.

THE FIX (services/tunnel/debuggTransport.ts)
The session and its 'stream' and 'error' listeners are now created synchronously with the socket, before the handshake can deliver anything. adopt() keeps only the lifecycle wiring ('goaway', 'close' -> reconnect), which must NOT fire for a session that never entered service. A failed handshake now tears the session down through a single `abandon()` helper: a socket that reached 101 is closed politely with a protocol code, and one that never upgraded is aborted — which `ws` also requires once an 'unexpected-response' listener is registered, since it then stops cleaning up the socket itself.

REGRESSION TEST
__tests__/services/debuggTransport.test.ts — "a stream that arrives in the SAME TICK as the handshake is not dropped": accept the handshake and deliver OPEN + DATA with no await in between, then assert the real loopback app received the request. Verified RED on the unfixed code ("Received array: []" — the request vanished) and green after.

HARNESS HARDENING (same class of bug, prompted by the server arc)
__tests__/integration/debuggTunnelServer.ts hand-rolled the server side and ignored WINDOW when sending, so a browser-to-app upload larger than one window would have been truncated while the test stayed green. It now drives the REAL TunnelSession in its 'server' role and pipes streams, so flow control is the protocol's, not the harness's. A new integration test uploads 3 MiB (about 12 windows) and asserts the app received every byte, complementing the existing 4 MiB download.
close_reason: Fixed: the session and its 'stream'/'error' listeners are now attached synchronously with the socket, so a frame arriving in the handshake tick is handled. Regression test verified RED on the unfixed code (the request vanished: 'Received array: []'), and a mutation putting just the 'stream' listener back into adopt() fails that test and only that test. The integration harness was also rebuilt on the real TunnelSession (server role) after the same class of bug — hand-rolled WINDOW handling — was reported by the server arc; a new 3 MiB upload test covers the direction it would have broken. Full suite 86/86, 1459 tests, tsc/lint/build clean, protocol arc's 236 intact.

design:
3.1 TECHNICAL STRATEGY — MCP tunnel client (confirmed 2026-09-19)

The failing suite from 2.1/2.2 is the definition of correct: 9 suites, 91 tests, 81 red, 9 green parity guards, 1 skipped (staging).

## 1. Pattern, and why
Strategy pattern behind one seam, chosen by data from the backend.
- `TunnelTransport` (services/tunnel/transport.ts) is the ONLY thing that differs between ngrok and debugg. Everything above it — handlers, tunnelContext, Caddy, PortLock, URL rewriting, the retry ladder, the idle timer, session keying — is untouched.
- The implementation is selected per tunnel from the provision response, never from an env var or a build flag, so rollout and rollback are server-side (design §2/§7). A response with no `transport` means ngrok, which is what keeps an old backend working against a new client.
- The seam is injected the way this repo already injects seams: public, overridable fields on TunnelManager (`caddyFactory`, `agentSessionStarter`, `connectBackoffMs`, `idleTimeoutMs`). A `transports` map joins them, so tests drive fakes with no module mocking.
- CONFIRMED starting point from the bead: extract the interface FIRST as a pure refactor with the ngrok tests untouched, then add the debugg implementation. Anything that moves in step 1 and changes an existing expectation is a bug in the refactor, not a new requirement.

## 2. Build vs reuse
Reuse:
- `ws` — pure JS, no binary, no postinstall. The only new dependency (the protocol agent owns package.json; it also needs @types/ws, or `npx tsc --noEmit` fails TS7016).
- services/tunnel/protocol/ — the shared module both ends of the wire speak.
- Everything already load-bearing: the 3-attempt retry ladder, FaultInjector/TunnelTrace, the 55-minute idle timer, per-session Caddy + PortLock, the registry, telemetry, tunnelDisposition's policy.
Build (small, and only here):
- ngrokTransport (a move, not new code), debuggTransport, the probe registry, known-domain handling, provision/revoke transport awareness.
Explicitly NOT built: a second tunnel manager, a parallel handler path, a client-side fallback between transports, any new binary.

## 3. Order the tests go green
Each step is independently shippable and keeps the whole suite green except for the tests that are still waiting on a later step.
0. package.json: ws + @types/ws (protocol arc).
1. PURE REFACTOR — extract TunnelTransport, move the ngrok-only steps into ngrokTransport: the lazy `import('ngrok')`, ensureInitialized/getApi, the ngrokAgentSession pre-warm, disconnect, the agent reset between attempts 1 and 2, and the reset-when-no-tunnels-remain. Zero test edits. The existing tunnelManager.test.ts / agentReadiness / concurrent suites are the regression gate. Turns nothing green on purpose.
2. Known tunnel domains (urlParser + TunnelManager) -> tunnelDomains.test.ts green. No transport needed; pure and isolated.
3. Markers and disposition (extractNgrokErrorCode's explicit marker list, the ENDPOINT_GONE allowlist, the ladder-confirm set) -> tunnelDisposition.debugg.test.ts and the marker half of localReachability.probe.test.ts green. Update the pinned allowlist assertion deliberately, as that test demands.
4. services/tunnels.ts: send `transports`, parse and validate the response, register the domain, transport-aware revoke -> tunnels.transport.test.ts green. Update the 3 exact-shape assertions in the existing tunnels.test.ts.
5. TunnelManager selection: the selection argument, the debugg hostname, the dedicated path using the PROVISIONED tunnel id, the transport telemetry tag, eviction on `onDead` -> tunnelManager.transport.test.ts green, driven by a FAKE transport. Still no ws.
6. debuggTransport on the protocol session + ws -> debuggTransport.test.ts green. Needs protocol 4.1 (xkoh.1.7).
7. Probe routing: the probe registry plus probeTunnelHealth's host-based lookup -> the rest of localReachability.probe.test.ts green.
8. (4.2) Handler plumbing: the 4 handlers pass the provision through and revoke by transport -> the integration suites green.
Steps 2-4 can land before step 1 if the refactor needs to wait; they touch nothing the refactor moves.

## 4. Risks and mitigations
R1 The refactor silently changes ngrok behaviour. Mitigation: step 1 edits no test; the ngrok suites must pass unchanged, including the agent-readiness and fault-injection ones. The public test seams keep their names and types.
R2 `ngrok` gets imported on the debugg path, so a Docker user still downloads a binary. Mitigation: the import-counter assertion in tunnelManager.transport.test.ts ("expected 0 loads") fails if any code path touches it.
R3 Flow control stalls a big dev-server chunk. Mitigation: the protocol arc's own tests plus the real-app integration test; the escalation path is already recorded on xkoh.1.2 (raise INITIAL_WINDOW in v2 or negotiate it — never hand-tune one side).
R4 A reconnect storm against the backend. Mitigation: 401/400/426 and GOAWAY(REVOKED) are terminal, backoff is capped, and `onDead` evicts the tunnel so the next call re-provisions instead of looping.
R5 A tunnel URL leaks to a caller because a domain is not "known". Mitigation: both domains are built in, a provisioned tunnelDomain is registered at runtime, the domain is validated (>= 3 labels) so it can never be broad enough to rewrite real links, and the handler integration test asserts the response carries no tunnel host.
R6 A tunnel older than its token's expiry cannot reconnect after a tunnel-server deploy, so a long session dies mid-run. Recorded as a cross-arc question on xkoh.5.2; the client already degrades safely (evict, re-provision next call).
R7 Open handles / zombie processes: an unclosed websocket or a ref'd ping timer would keep the MCP alive after its client exits. Mitigation: unref the ping and reconnect timers; stopAllTunnels closes the sockets on SIGINT/SIGTERM; verify at 5.1 with --detectOpenHandles, because jest's forceExit hides this class of bug.
R8 Both transports alive in one process (a session tunnel on one, a test_suite dedicated tunnel on the other). Mitigation: the ngrok module reset counts only ngrok tunnels, and disconnect/probe route through the tunnel's own recorded transport.
R9 Deliberate red at 4.1 in three existing assertions (the provision request body and result object in tunnels.test.ts, the allowlist membership in tunnelDisposition.test.ts). They are contract changes, not regressions, and each must be updated with its step.
R10 The integration suites need BOTH arcs. Mitigation: they carry a fail-fast seam guard so a partial state reports "no debugg transport" instead of falling through to the real ngrok agent.

## 5. Rollback
- Primary: the backend flag. It stops selecting "debugg", every new tunnel is ngrok again, and no MCP release is involved. Existing debugg tunnels keep working until they idle out.
- Secondary: ngrokTransport stays in the package for the whole migration; deleting it is the rollout arc's last step (design §7.7).
- There is deliberately NO client-side fallback: a debugg token cannot drive ngrok, and an automatic fallback would mask a server outage and double-provision. A failed debugg connect surfaces today's TunnelCreationFailed and the next call re-provisions.
- Blast radius if the debugg path is wrong: localhost testing only. Public-URL targets and dev mode never tunnel.
close_reason: Strategy recorded: strategy pattern behind one TunnelTransport seam selected by the provision response; pure ngrok extraction first with zero test edits, then 7 ordered steps to green; 10 risks with mitigations; rollback is the backend flag with no client-side fallback.

title: [tunnel-mcp-client] 3.2 Architecture & Interface Design
description:
Define module boundaries, interface contracts, data flow and file locations. Follow existing patterns in the target repo; don't invent new ones. Record with `--design`.

Arc specifics:
Confirm the services/tunnel/ layout (transport.ts, ngrokTransport.ts, debuggTransport.ts, protocol/), where
the known-domains config lives, and where PROBE plugs into utils/localReachability.ts.

Repo: debugg-ai-mcp. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §5. Arc epic: debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.5.
design:
3.2 ARCHITECTURE & INTERFACE DESIGN — MCP tunnel client (confirmed 2026-09-19) Follows the repo's existing patterns: one directory per concern under services/, pure helpers in utils/, seams as public overridable fields, and no new env vars. ## 1. File layout services/tunnel/ protocol/ OWNED BY THE PROTOCOL ARC (xkoh.1): constants, errors, codec, handshake, transport, stream, session, index, vectors. node: built-ins only, no imports from this repo. Its index.ts is the ONLY entry point — xkoh.1.6's rule is that neither arc imports below it, and every stub and test in this arc follows that. transport.ts The TunnelTransport interface and the selection types. Types only — no logic, no runtime imports beyond protocol types. ngrokTransport.ts Today's ngrok code, moved verbatim: the lazy import('ngrok'), getApi() init, the ngrokAgentSession pre-warm, connect/disconnect, the agent reset hook, and the reset-when-no-tunnels-remain hook. debuggTransport.ts The websocket client: it owns the socket lifecycle and composes the protocol module rather than reimplementing it. Uses `ws` (now in package.json, with @types/ws) and TunnelSession. probeRegistry.ts host -> ControlProbe, written by debuggTransport, read by probeTunnelHealth. utils/ tunnelDomains.ts NEW. The known tunnel domains and their transport kind. services/ngrok/ tunnelManager.ts STAYS HERE in v1, importing the transports. Moving it to services/tunnel/ would churn ~10 import sites and 4 test files for no behavioural gain; it moves in the ngrok-deletion step (design §7.7), when services/ngrok/ disappears entirely. Why services/tunnel/ rather than extending services/ngrok/: the directory name is the transport name. Putting a debugg client under services/ngrok/ would make the ngrok deletion step a rename instead of a delete. ## 2. Interfaces ### TunnelTransport (services/tunnel/transport.ts) kind: 'ngrok' | 'debugg' connect(localAddr, hostname, token, opts) -> Promise disconnect(publicUrl) -> Promise probe?(publicUrl, path, {timeoutMs}) -> Promise // debugg only prepare?(token) -> Promise // ngrok pre-warm resetAfterFailedAttempt?() -> Promise // ngrok agent reset, between ladder attempts 1 and 2 onAllTunnelsStopped?() -> void // ngrok module reset opts = { tunnelId, relayUrl?, onDead?(reason) } Contract points: - `localAddr` is the ONLY address the tunnel may dial, for its whole life. Five accepted forms: Caddy's http://127.0.0.1:

(session tunnels, including in Docker), and 127.0.0.1:

/ host.docker.internal:

/ https://localhost:

/ https://host.docker.internal:

(the dedicated test_suite path). An https:// form dials TLS without verifying the certificate, matching Caddy's insecure_skip_verify for local self-signed certs. - connect returns a path-free origin. The public URL is a property of the tunnel id, not of a socket, so it survives every reconnect. - Errors carry `retryable`. false means terminal for this token (401, 400, 426); everything else is left to TunnelManager's existing ladder. - `onDead` is the only upward callback. It means "this tunnel can never come back" (revoked, or auth failed on reconnect); TunnelManager reacts by evicting through its normal stopTunnel path. - The optional hooks exist so the retry ladder can stay in TunnelManager and stay transport-neutral. ngrok implements them; debugg implements none. ### TunnelTransportSelection { transport, relayUrl?, tunnelDomain?, tunnelId? } A TunnelProvision satisfies it structurally, so callers pass the provision itself. Absent means ngrok. ### How debuggTransport composes the protocol module (xkoh.1.6) ws socket (via the socketFactory seam) -> webSocketTransport(ws) protocol/transport.ts: the FrameTransport adapter, the only place that knows a websocket exists -> new TunnelSession(transport, {role:'client'}) buildHandshakeHeaders(...) builds the request headers; interpretHandshakeResponse(...) decides accepted vs rejected from the 101 echo or the 400/401/426 body. This transport adds nothing to the wire: it contributes the socket, the reconnect policy, the dial policy and the registry entry. Session events map straight onto this arc's responsibilities: 'stream' -> dial ONLY localAddr and pipe both directions; a dial failure is stream.reset(UPSTREAM_UNREACHABLE) 'goaway' -> reconnect make-before-break, unless the code is REVOKED, which is terminal -> onDead 'close' -> reconnect with backoff, unless the handshake said 401/400/426 -> onDead probe() delegates to TunnelSession.probe(path, {timeoutMs}), which already guarantees the never-throws contract ({error:'TIMEOUT'} on a deadline, {error:'CLOSED'} on a closed session). So the registered ControlProbe is just the live session's probe, and this arc owns only the mapping onto TunnelHealthProbeResult. ### ControlProbe (services/tunnel/probeRegistry.ts) (path, {timeoutMs}) -> Promise // never throws; a failure is a ProbeResult registerControlProbe(host, probe) / unregisterControlProbe(host) / getControlProbe(url) Keyed by the public host (.tunnel.debugg.ai), written on connect and removed on disconnect. Module-level state, like the template caches in utils/handlerCaches.ts. ### utils/tunnelDomains.ts Built-ins: ngrok.debugg.ai -> 'ngrok', tunnel.debugg.ai -> 'debugg'. registerTunnelDomain(domain, transport) // called by provision, so a server-side domain move needs no release tunnelDomainFor(host) -> { domain, transport } | undefined isTunnelHost(host) / knownTunnelDomains() Validation: lowercase DNS name, >= 3 labels. A 2-label value like "debugg.ai" would make replaceTunnelUrls rewrite real product links into localhost. It lives in utils/ and imports NOTHING, so utils/urlParser.ts (which imports nothing today), services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts and utils/localReachability.ts can all use it with no cycle. services/tunnel/ stays transport mechanics only. ## 3. Data flow Creation (session tunnel) handler -> client.tunnels.provisionWithRetry() -> tunnels.ts validates, registers the tunnelDomain, returns TunnelProvision{transport,...} handler -> ensureTunnel(ctx, key, id, keyId, revoke, provision) -> tunnelManager.ensureSessionTunnel(sessionKey, ..., selection) -> caddy.ensureStarted() -> localOrigin -> connectWithRetry(localOrigin, `${id}.${domain}`, token, selection) transport = this.transports[selection.transport] transport.prepare?.() // ngrok only transport.connect(...) // ngrok.connect(), or the websocket handshake -> TunnelInfo{ transport, tunnelUrl, caddy, portLock, ... } Browser request (debugg) browser -> .tunnel.debugg.ai -> ALB -> nginx -> tunnel server -> OPEN/DATA over the control socket -> debuggTransport dials ONLY localAddr -> Caddy -> the app, and pipes the bytes back Health probe handler -> probeTunnelHealth(targetUrl) -> tunnelDomainFor(host).transport === 'debugg' ? getControlProbe(url) : http1Fetch -> PROBE {path + search} -> PROBE_RESULT -> mapped to TunnelHealthProbeResult -> disposition decides eviction from ngrokErrorCode, unchanged Teardown stopTunnel -> unconditional map removal (unchanged) -> allSettled[ transport.disconnect(url), caddy.stop(), revokeKey() ] -> transport.onAllTunnelsStopped?.() when no tunnels of that kind remain ## 4. Where PROBE plugs into utils/localReachability.ts - probeTunnelHealth keeps its exact signature, its retry ladder, its timeouts and its result type. All five call sites are untouched. - Inside probeOnce, the SOURCE becomes conditional: a control probe for a debugg tunnel host, http1Fetch otherwise. Everything downstream (the ladder, the confirm-across-retries rule for OFFLINE/ERR_NGROK_3200, the disposition allowlist) is shared by both. - A debugg host with no registered prober resolves as DEBUGG_TUNNEL_UNKNOWN rather than being fetched: the URL is private, and no live control channel in this process means the tunnel is not coming back on its own. - Mapping (from xkoh.1.2 §9, not re-derived): status without a marker -> healthy; 502/504 without a marker -> BAD_GATEWAY; any marker -> code 'NGROK_ERROR' + ngrokErrorCode; error "TIMEOUT" -> TIMEOUT; any other error -> NETWORK_ERROR with the detail. - The result field names keep their ngrok spelling in v1 (`code:'NGROK_ERROR'`, `ngrokErrorCode`) because handlers echo them into tool output; renaming is part of the ngrok deletion. ## 5. Configuration No new env vars. The transport, the relay URL and the tunnel domain are all data from the provision response, which is what makes rollout and rollback server-side. X-Debugg-Tunnel-Client-Version comes from config.server.version, which is already the package version. The existing DEBUGG_TUNNEL_FAULT_MODE fault injection keeps working because it lives in the ladder, above the transport. Only the tests introduce env vars (DEBUGGAI_STAGING_API_KEY / _URL), and only to opt IN to the live test. ## 6. Protocol-module consumption (settled by xkoh.1.6) xkoh.1.6 chose a VENDORED COPY in the server's repo, gated by the same conformance vectors, over an npm subpath export of @debugg-ai/debugg-ai-mcp. That is the right call for this arc too: a subpath export would have needed an `exports` map, and adding one restricts the deep imports this package's consumers use today. Nothing changes here — this arc imports services/tunnel/protocol/index.js by relative path either way. The only standing requirement from this side is that the module keeps its "node: built-ins only" property, because this arc is what wraps `ws` around it; the sync script and the two CI vector gates belong to the protocol arc.
close_reason: Architecture recorded and reconciled with the protocol arc's xkoh.1.6: services/tunnel/{transport,ngrokTransport,debuggTransport,probeRegistry}.ts plus utils/tunnelDomains.ts, with tunnelManager.ts deliberately left in services/ngrok/ until the ngrok deletion step. debuggTransport composes webSocketTransport + TunnelSession(role:'client') + the handshake helpers and imports only protocol/index.js. PROBE plugs into probeOnce as a conditional source, leaving probeTunnelHealth's signature, ladder and result type untouched. No new env vars.

title: [tunnel-mcp-client] 4.1 Core Implementation
description:
Write the minimum code to make the failing unit tests pass. Run the suite after each meaningful change. No extra features, refactors or 'improvements' beyond what the tests cover. Notes: X/Y unit tests passing.

Repo: debugg-ai-mcp. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §5. Arc epic: debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.5.
notes:
4.1 CORE IMPLEMENTATION — done. Every test from 2.1 and 2.2 is green.

RUN (worktree tunnel/debugg-transport):
  npm test            -> 86 suites passed, 1 skipped; 1457 passed, 2 skipped, 0 failed
  npx tsc --noEmit    -> clean
  npm run lint        -> clean
  npm run build       -> clean
Baseline before the arc was 72 suites / 1126 passed, and all 72 still pass.

## What was written
- utils/tunnelDomains.ts (new) — the known tunnel domains and their transport, built-ins plus runtime registration from a provision response, with a >= 3-label validation rule so a registered domain can never be broad enough to rewrite real product links. Imports nothing, so urlParser/localReachability/tunnelManager can all use it without a cycle.
- utils/urlParser.ts — replaceTunnelUrls rewrites every known domain instead of a hardcoded ngrok one. generateTunnelUrl already took a domain; its caller now passes one.
- utils/localReachability.ts — extractNgrokErrorCode reads the three DEBUGG_TUNNEL_* markers from an EXPLICIT list (a prefix pattern would match our own DEBUGG_TUNNEL_FAULT_MODE env var in run evidence); probeOnce routes a debugg tunnel host through the control channel and maps PROBE_RESULT per xkoh.1.2 §9; DEBUGG_TUNNEL_OFFLINE joins the confirm-across-the-ladder set while UNKNOWN stays definitive.
- utils/tunnelDisposition.ts — the ENDPOINT_GONE allowlist adds OFFLINE and UNKNOWN; UPSTREAM_REFUSED stays out for the same reason ERR_NGROK_8012 does.
- services/tunnel/transport.ts — the TunnelTransport interface, its selection type, and the three ngrok-only hooks that let the retry ladder stay transport-neutral.
- services/tunnel/ngrokTransport.ts (new) — today's ngrok code, MOVED: the lazy import('ngrok'), the getApi bootstrap, the pqgj agent pre-warm, connect/disconnect, the agent reset between ladder attempts, and the reset-when-no-tunnels-remain. Nothing on the debugg path can now reach the ngrok package.
- services/tunnel/debuggTransport.ts — the websocket client. It composes the protocol module (buildHandshakeHeaders / interpretHandshakeResponse / webSocketTransport / TunnelSession role:'client') and owns only the socket, the reconnect policy, the dial policy and the registry entry.
- services/tunnel/probeRegistry.ts — host -> prober, written by the transport, read by probeTunnelHealth, so the probe seam needed no change to probeTunnelHealth's signature or its five call sites.
- services/tunnels.ts — sends transports ["debugg","ngrok"]; a response without `transport` means ngrok; validates a debugg response (relayUrl must be wss except on loopback, tunnelDomain must be usable) and registers its domain; revoke() routes ngrok keys to api/v1/ngrok/revoke/ and debugg tunnels to api/v1/tunnels/<id>/revoke/.
- services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts — a `transports` map (public, like caddyFactory), the selection threaded through ensureSessionTunnel/createSessionTunnel/acquireDedicatedTunnel, the ladder driven through the transport with `retryable:false` honoured, eviction when a transport reports the tunnel permanently dead, transport-tagged telemetry, per-transport "no tunnels remain" notification, and isTunnelUrl/extractTunnelId reading the domain registry. agentSessionStarter/agentSessionTimeoutMs remain as accessors so the existing suites keep driving them.
- utils/tunnelContext.ts — ensureTunnel takes and forwards the selection (optional; omitted means ngrok).
- handlers (all four) — pass the provision through and revoke by transport. Mechanical, approved by the owner.

## Contract checks against the other arcs
- Backend (xkoh.2.2/2.7): POST api/v1/tunnels/ {purpose, transports}; camelCase response carrying transport/relayUrl/tunnelDomain; POST api/v1/tunnels/<id>/revoke/. Matches. `transports` is a single word so the MCP's snake_casing leaves it alone, and objToSnakeCase leaves string array entries untouched (verified).
- Protocol (xkoh.1.2/1.6): imports only services/tunnel/protocol/index.js, never below it.
- expires_at gates the FIRST connect only (owner decision): the client never expires a tunnel of its own accord. Only a server rejection (401/400/426) or GOAWAY(REVOKED) ends one, and a test drives three drop/reconnect cycles asserting the same token goes back each time and onDead never fires.

## The blocked-egress message (owner asked for the exact wording)
Verbatim, for a pre-upgrade connection failure:
  "could not reach the debugg tunnel server at <relayHost> (<CODE>: <detail>). Testing a local app needs a direct outbound HTTPS connection to <relayHost> on port 443 — allow it in your firewall, VPN or container network rules.<proxyNote>"
where proxyNote is either
  " This environment sets <HTTPS_PROXY|https_proxy|ALL_PROXY|all_proxy>, which the tunnel connection does NOT use — HTTP(S) proxies are not supported for it."
or, when no proxy variable is set,
  " HTTP(S) proxies are not supported for the tunnel connection."
It stays retryable (egress can be restored without re-provisioning). A 407 gets its own terminal message naming the intercepting proxy. Two unit tests pin the host, the port, the outbound wording and the proxy note.

## Existing tests updated deliberately (contract changes, not regressions)
- __tests__/services/tunnels.test.ts — 4 exact-shape assertions: the request body now carries `transports`, and the result carries `transport: 'ngrok'`.
- __tests__/utils/tunnelDisposition.test.ts — the pinned allowlist now lists the two debugg codes. This is exactly the deliberate act that assertion exists to force.
- __tests__/utils/tunnelContext.test.ts — two ensureSessionTunnel call assertions gained the trailing selection argument.
- __tests__/handlers/runTestSuiteHandler.test.ts — acquireDedicatedTunnel is called with the provision, because a debugg token is bound to the id the backend issued.
- __tests__/handlers/testPageChangesHandler.test.ts — the three revoke assertions moved from revokeNgrokKey to the transport-aware tunnels.revoke.
No other existing test was touched. The whole pre-existing ngrok suite (tunnelManager, agentReadiness, concurrent, caddy, portLock) passes unchanged, which is the gate the pure-refactor step was designed around.

## Deliberately NOT done
probePageHandler's orphan-revoke condition (`tc && !tc.tunnelId`) still does not fire when ensureTunnel throws, so a provisioned tunnel leaks until it expires. Owner filed it as debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.9 and scoped it out of this arc; only the endpoint the revoke targets changed here. The integration test pins TODAY's behaviour and names the bead, so whoever takes xkoh.9 flips it.
close_reason: Core implementation green: every 2.1/2.2 test passes (86 suites, 1457 tests, 0 failures), tsc/lint/build clean, and the whole pre-existing ngrok suite passes unchanged — the pure-refactor gate held. TunnelTransport seam + ngrokTransport (a move) + debuggTransport on the protocol session, known-domain handling, the PROBE seam, markers/disposition, transport-aware revoke, and the four mechanical handler edits the owner approved.

title: [tunnel-mcp-client] MCP tunnel client — debugg transport behind a TunnelTransport interface
description:
Swap the ngrok.connect() step in TunnelManager for a TunnelTransport interface with two implementations, ngrok (kept during migration) and debugg (pure TS on the shared protocol plus `ws`). The backend's provision response picks the transport. Everything above the transport stays unchanged.

Repo: debugg-ai-mcp. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §5.
Test-first arc (feature-lifecycle): each phase is blocked by the one before it, and some phases are
blocked by phases in other arcs. Umbrella: debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.
notes:
FROM THE SERVER ARC'S INTEGRATION TESTS (xkoh.3.8, 2026-09-19) — a race the client MUST avoid:

Construct the TunnelSession (and attach its handlers) as soon as the WebSocket is CREATED, not
after 'open'. The tunnel server registers the tunnel the instant the websocket handshake
completes and may send OPEN immediately — on a reconnect there is often a browser request
already waiting out its 5 s grace window. A client that waits for 'open' before attaching drops
those first frames, and that request hangs until the browser gives up.

It is invisible to unit tests (they drive frames by hand) and to a first connect (no traffic is
waiting yet). It showed up only in the reconnect-gap integration test, where it looked like a
30 s hang. The server arc's harness now attaches at construction time; debuggTransport should do
the same.
close_reason: Arc complete: all 12 phases shipped and verified in production (mcp-client).

title: [tunnel-mcp-client] 1.1 User Requirements
description:
Capture who the user is, the problem, acceptance criteria (when is this done?), and non-goals. Pre-filled below from the design and the owner's decisions: confirm or adjust, then record with `bd update <id> --notes=...` and close.

Arc specifics:
- Who: every MCP user testing a localhost app with check_app_in_browser, probe_page, trigger_crawl or
  test_suite run.
- Problem: the MCP's tunnel service depends on ngrok (a binary download, ngrok-specific errors, keys minted
  by ngrok).
- Acceptance: when the backend selects the debugg transport, localhost testing behaves as it does today,
  through tunnel.debugg.ai: no new install steps, no binaries, works in Docker, same tool outputs (tunnel
  URLs never leak to callers). When the backend selects ngrok, or the backend is old, behavior is exactly

- Non-goals: removing ngrok code (rollout arc); dropping Caddy (follow-up); tunneling over the HTTP
  (remote MCP) transport.

Repo: debugg-ai-mcp. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §5. Arc epic: debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.5.
notes:

- Errors are ngrok-specific (ERR_NGROK_*). Keys are minted by ngrok through the backend (api/v1/tunnels/ → ngrok_api.py) and revoked through api/v1/ngrok/revoke/.

ACCEPTANCE (confirmed, with corrections marked [C])
A1. When the backend's provision response selects transport "debugg":
    - localhost testing works end-to-end through https://<tunnelId>.tunnel.debugg.ai for all four tools.
    - No binary download or spawn. `ngrok` is never imported and the ngrok agent is never started on that path.
    - No new install steps. `caddy` on PATH is still required for the three Caddy-routed tools, exactly as today; test_suite run still does not need it.
A2. Works in Docker:
    - Session tunnels dial Caddy's in-container loopback origin (http://127.0.0.1:<proxyPort>), unchanged.
    - The dedicated path dials host.docker.internal:<port> per the existing matrix.
    - The only egress needed is wss to the relayUrl host (api.debugg.ai:443), the same host the MCP already talks to.
A3. Same tool outputs:
    - No tunnel hostname of either domain ever reaches a caller. sanitizeResponseUrls must rewrite *.ngrok.debugg.ai AND *.tunnel.debugg.ai.
    - Error payload shapes stay identical (TunnelTrafficBlocked, TunnelOfflineDuringRun, TunnelCreationFailed, TunnelProvisionFailed, LocalServerUnreachable), including the `detail.ngrokErrorCode` field name.
    - [C] One user-visible copy change is needed: testPageChangesHandler.ts ~L906-914 hardcodes "ngrok error page" / "ngrok's <code> interstitial". It must become transport-neutral when the marker is DEBUGG_TUNNEL_*.
A4. When the backend selects "ngrok", or omits `transport` because it is an old backend, behavior is byte-for-byte today's: same ngrok.connect options, pre-warm, retry ladder and revoke endpoint.
A5. [C] TunnelManager API: "unchanged" means ADDITIVE ONLY, i.e. optional trailing parameters or an options object.
    - Every existing call signature (ensureSessionTunnel, acquireDedicatedTunnel, stopTunnel, markTunnelDead, getSessionTunnelInfo, getTunnelInfo, touchTunnel, the public test seams connectBackoffMs / agentSessionStarter / agentSessionTimeoutMs / caddyFactory / idleTimeoutMs) keeps compiling and keeps meaning ngrok.
    - Handlers' tunnel LOGIC is unchanged. But the provision response's transport fields must physically reach TunnelManager, and today the handlers pass tunnelKey/tunnelId/keyId positionally.
    - So the 4 handler call sites need a mechanical plumbing change: pass the provision through, and use a transport-aware revoke. Details are in 1.2 (R2, R9).
A6. tunnelContext, Caddy (services/caddy/caddyProxy.ts), PortLock (services/caddy/portLock.ts), session keying (getSessionKey), the idle timer (55 min) and the cold-start dedup are unchanged.
A7. Rollback needs no MCP release: the backend flips the flag back to ngrok.

NON-GOALS (confirmed, plus additions)
- Removing ngrok code: ngrokTransport, ngrokAgentSession.ts, ngrok-config.yml, the ngrok dependency (rollout arc, step 7).
- Dropping Caddy/PortLock (port-in-hostname follow-up).

- [added] services/ngrok/ngrokAgentInspector.ts, which has no production importer, and its OWNED_TUNNEL_SUFFIX '.ngrok.debugg.ai'. It stays ngrok-only.
- [added] Tunnel-server, nginx and backend (sentinal) changes, which belong to other arcs.
- [added] Renaming ngrok-named identifiers (ngrokErrorCode, code 'NGROK_ERROR', ENDPOINT_GONE_NGROK_CODES, services/ngrok/ directory) in v1. Renames would change tool output shape, so they are deferred to the ngrok-deletion step.

WHO IS NOT AFFECTED: public-URL targets, dev mode, and all non-browser tools (project, environment, test_case, executions).
