title: [tunnel-mcp-client] 2.2 Write Failing Integration Tests
description:
Write integration tests for the paths that cross boundaries. Confirm they fail. Record the count in notes.

Arc specifics:
- in-process fake tunnel server (built on the protocol module) + real Caddy + a local HTTP app: the
  handler-level check_app_in_browser / probe_page path reaches the app through the debugg transport
  (backend mocked)
- a live test in `npm run test:integration` against staging that skips itself without a staging key

Repo: debugg-ai-mcp. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §5. Arc epic: debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.5.
notes:
2.2 FAILING INTEGRATION TESTS: written and confirmed RED (worktree tunnel/debugg-transport, 2026-09-19)

## Run summary
This bead's files: 3 suites, 9 tests — 8 red, 1 skipped (the staging one, correctly self-skipping with no staging key).
Whole arc so far (2.1 + 2.2): 9 suites, 91 tests — 81 red, 9 green guards, 1 skipped.
Whole repo: 72 pre-existing suites still pass, unchanged from the baseline. The other red suites belong to the protocol arc (xkoh.1.3). npx tsc --noEmit clean; npm run lint clean.

## Files
- __tests__/integration/debuggTunnelServer.ts — NOT a test file (jest collects *.test.ts). An in-process debugg tunnel SERVER built on the shared protocol module: a control websocket (ws, perMessageDeflate off, maxPayload MAX_FRAME_SIZE, echoing X-Debugg-Tunnel-Protocol on the 101) and a raw-TCP ingress where one browser connection becomes one stream. It answers PROBE by issuing a real GET back through its own ingress, and renders the DEBUGG_TUNNEL_* marker pages (body AND X-Debugg-Tunnel-Error header) that the client parses. `authorize` lets a test force 401/426; `goaway()` simulates the SIGTERM deploy path.
  Deliberately built on services/tunnel/protocol/ rather than hand-rolled: the point of the shared module is that both ends speak it, and the fake server is the first consumer proving that.

- __tests__/integration/debuggTunnel.test.ts — 6 tests, all red. Real TunnelManager, real debugg transport, REAL caddy process, real local HTTP app; only the tunnel server is faked and the backend is absent (the provision response is simulated as a transport selection).
  1. a browser request reaches the local app through the tunnel and Caddy;
  2. the handshake carried Authorization: Bearer, X-Debugg-Tunnel-Id and X-Debugg-Tunnel-Protocol, with no secret in the URL;
  3. probeTunnelHealth answers over the control channel, with an injected fetch that throws if the private host is ever fetched;
  4. with the app stopped, Caddy's markerless 502 maps to BAD_GATEWAY and the tunnel is KEPT (the ERR_NGROK_8012 lesson, carried over);
  5. a GOAWAY mid-session reconnects and the next browser request still works, same URL — the deploy case from design §3;
  6. stopTunnel closes the control socket and tears down that session's Caddy.
  Self-skips (describe.skip) when `caddy` is not on PATH, like __tests__/integration/caddyProxy.test.ts, because this directory runs under `npm test` too.

- __tests__/integration/debuggTunnel.handler.test.ts — 2 tests, both red. probe_page at the handler level with ONLY the backend mocked (provision, template lookup, executeWorkflow, pollExecution). The fake backend plays the remote browser by fetching the tunnel URL it was handed, through the fake ingress.
  1. the backend receives contextData.targetUrl on the tunnel domain (not localhost), the request travels tunnel -> transport -> Caddy -> app, and the handler's response mentions no tunnel hostname while reporting the caller's own localhost URL — the sanitizer working against the NEW domain;
  2. a tunnel that never connects (server forced to 401) is revoked through the debugg endpoint, not revokeNgrokKey — this pins the handler plumbing from xkoh.5.2 R2/R9, which nothing else can test.

- __tests__/integration/debuggTunnel.staging.test.ts — 1 test, skipped here. Provision -> connect -> serve -> PROBE -> revoke against a live staging backend and tunnel server. Self-skips unless BOTH DEBUGGAI_STAGING_API_KEY and DEBUGGAI_STAGING_API_URL are set, so it can never run against prod or by accident (provision and revoke are writes). If staging still selects the ngrok transport it logs and returns rather than failing.

## Red for the right reason
All 8 report the same missing thing: TunnelManager has no transport seam, so a debugg selection is ignored.
A fail-fast guard runs first in both suites (`expect(typeof tunnelManager.transports?.debugg?.connect).toBe('function')` -> "Expected: function, Received: undefined"). It was added after the first run showed the fall-through calling the REAL ngrok agent: without the guard a red run spawns the ngrok binary and hits ngrok's API (observed: "connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:4043" and "invalid tunnel configuration", ~6s per test). The guard keeps the red phase hermetic and becomes a no-op once 4.1 lands.

## Notes for 4.2
- `ws` is imported through a namespace with a runtime fallback (ws.WebSocketServer ?? ws.default?.WebSocketServer ?? ws.Server), because `ws` is CommonJS and jest's ESM interop does not reliably hand back module.exports as the default. Keep that shape, or switch to createRequire.
- The handler test's pollExecution fixture matches today's browser.capture outputData contract (capturedUrl, statusCode, title, loadTimeMs, consoleSlice, networkSummary). If the handler's formatting contract changes, the fixture needs updating with it — that is a fixture fix, not a tunnel regression.
- These integration tests need BOTH arcs: the protocol session (xkoh.1.7) and this arc's transport (xkoh.5.7). They stay red until both land, which is exactly what 4.2 is for.

## ADDENDUM — a pre-existing bug the handler test #2 also requires
probePageHandler's orphan-revoke loop (~L536) reads:
  for (i...) { const keyId = acquiredKeyIds[i]; const tc = targetContexts[i]; if (tc && !tc.tunnelId && keyId) revoke }
When ensureTunnel throws, `targetContexts.push(tunneled)` never runs, so targetContexts[i] is undefined, `tc` is falsy and NO revoke fires — today, on the ngrok path too. VERIFIED as probe_page-only: triggerCrawlHandler (L404) and testPageChangesHandler (L1067) use `if (!ctx.tunnelId && keyId)` over a single ctx and DO fire, and runTestSuiteHandler (L175) uses `acquiredKeyId && !tunnelId` and fires too. Only probePageHandler indexes an array that the failure path never filled, because it is the batch handler.
So "a tunnel that never connects is revoked through the debugg endpoint" needs two things in 4.2: the transport-aware revoke (xkoh.5.2 R9) AND that guard fixed so the orphan revoke fires when tunnel creation fails. Both belong to the revoke work; neither is a regression from this arc. The test carries the same note inline so it cannot be mistaken for a routing-only failure.
Also: the fake backend client records only — no expect() inside it, because those calls run inside the handler's try/catch and .catch() paths where a failed assertion would be swallowed or resurface as an unrelated MCPError. The test body does the asserting.

## ADDENDUM — reconciled with the protocol architecture (xkoh.1.6)
The protocol module gained services/tunnel/protocol/index.ts as its ONLY public surface ("neither arc imports below index.ts"). The fake server helper and every test and stub in this arc now import from protocol/index.js rather than from codec.ts / constants.ts / transport.ts directly. Counts after the change are unchanged: 8 suites red (81 tests), 1 skipped, 9 green guards; tsc and lint clean.
close_reason: 3 integration files: an in-process tunnel server built on the shared protocol module driving real Caddy + a real local app (6 red), probe_page at the handler level with only the backend mocked (2 red, pins the handler provision/revoke plumbing), and a live staging test that self-skips without staging creds. Pre-existing 72 suites still green; tsc and lint clean.

WIRING DONE IN THIS PHASE
- The four handlers pass the provision through and revoke by transport (approved as mechanical).

Repo: platform. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §3. Arc epic: debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.3.
notes:
4.2 INTEGRATION IMPLEMENTATION — DONE, integration suite GREEN (2026-09-19, server-arc agent).

  npm run test:integration   3 suites, 29 tests: 25 passed, 4 skipped (the live-stack suite)
  Runtime fell from ~37 s (hanging teardowns) to ~7 s once the bugs below were fixed.
  npm test                   186 passed   ·   npx tsc --noEmit clean   ·   build clean

WHAT THESE TESTS ACTUALLY EXERCISE NOW
A real websocket, the REAL protocol client session (TunnelSession role 'client', the same class
the MCP will use), the real codec and its credit accounting, a real local app, and two real
server instances forwarding to each other. Only two things are doubled: the debugg API (an HTTP
stand-in that checks the service token and can be made to reject or break) and Redis (an
in-process transport that publishes the real payload on the real subscriber).

FOUR BUGS THE INTEGRATION TESTS CAUGHT — all real, none cosmetic
1. SHUTDOWN DEADLOCK (server bug, would have hit every prod deploy).
   stopAccepting() awaited server.close()'s CALLBACK, which fires only once every connection has
   gone — and the live tunnels cannot go until they have been told to, which happens AFTER
   stopAccepting in the lifecycle. A SIGTERM would have hung until ECS SIGKILLed the task at
   stopTimeout, cutting in-flight requests instead of draining them. Now: close() stops the
   listener immediately (which is what makes nginx's proxy_next_upstream move on), and only the
   final close() takes the remaining sockets.
2. BOOT BLOCKED ON REDIS (server bug). startTunnelServer awaited the Redis connect, and
   node-redis retries a refused connection indefinitely, so a Redis outage would have stopped the
   server from serving traffic it does not need Redis for. Now the subscribe is fire-and-forget
   behind a 5 s connect timeout, and a failure is a warning: the re-verify interval is the
   backstop that makes a lost revoke a latency bug, not a hole.
3. CLIENT ATTACH RACE (cross-arc finding, for the MCP client arc xkoh.5).
   The server registers the tunnel the instant the websocket handshake completes and may send
   OPEN immediately — a browser request may already be waiting out its grace window. A client
   that waits for 'open' before constructing its TunnelSession drops those first frames, and that
   request hangs until the browser gives up. The harness now attaches the session at construction
   time. THE MCP CLIENT MUST DO THE SAME; it is invisible to unit tests and only shows up in the
   reconnect-gap case.
4. HARNESS, not the server: a hand-rolled client that ignored WINDOW truncated a 2 MiB download
   at ~1.5 MB. Replacing it with the real protocol session fixed it — which is exactly the
   flowing-mode consumption class of bug the protocol arc hit, and the reason the suite carries a
   payload several times larger than one 256 KiB window.
   (Also harness-side: chunked bodies are now decoded, header lookups are lowercased, and
   upgraded sockets are tracked so teardown cannot hang.)

COVERAGE (25 green)
  tunnelTraffic (16): GET; Host byte-identical end to end; a 512 KiB POST; a 2 MiB download
    intact; chunked; SSE; a websocket upgrade (HMR) with its 101 and an echoed frame; 50 parallel
    requests on one tunnel with 50 distinct server-allocated stream ids; UPSTREAM_REFUSED when
    the app is down; PROBE returning a status and returning a marker; every connect verified with
    the service token; a broken API refusing the connect (fail closed); a rejected token refused;
    404 OFFLINE for an unconnected tunnel; 404 UNKNOWN for a Host outside the domain.
  twoTasks (9): ingress landing on the non-owner forwarded to the owner; the forwarded request
    byte-identical; OFFLINE when neither owns it; the tunnel following a client that reconnects to
    the other task; GOAWAY(GOING_AWAY) on shutdown; a 2 MiB download finishing while the task
    drains; the next request served by the new task; a draining task refusing new connects; and a
    browser request HELD through the reconnect gap rather than failed.
  Two instances find each other through the discovery seam, whose addresses may now carry an
  explicit ":port" — bare IPs in prod (every task listens on 8080), host:port locally.

LIVE STACK (4 tests, still gated on TUNNEL_SERVER_LIVE_STACK=1)
Not runnable from this worktree, and not because of this code: the tunnels endpoints live on the
tokens arc's branch (tunnel/tokens), while this worktree is tunnel/server — backend/config/urls.py
here has no /api/internal/ route at all. Docker is available; a tree with BOTH branches merged
would run it as:
  docker compose -f local.yml up -d django redis
  # provision a debugg-transport Tunnel, note its key, set TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN in django
  TUNNEL_SERVER_LIVE_STACK=1 LIVE_VERIFY_URL=... LIVE_REDIS_URL=... LIVE_TUNNEL_SERVICE_TOKEN=...
  LIVE_TUNNEL_ID=... LIVE_TUNNEL_KEY=... npm run test:integration
It covers a real verified connect, a token the real API rejects, a real revoke taking effect
through real Redis, and the periodic re-verify. Worth running at the integration point of the two
branches; the debugg-API half of the same contract is the tokens arc's own xkoh.2.4.

COMPOSE WIRING (owner-approved)
local.yml gains a profile-gated `tunnel-server` service (build context ./tunnel-server, host ports
8480/8481 because eval-app owns 8080, VERIFY_URL at django:8002 — the container port, not the 8012
host mapping — REDIS_URL at redis:6379, and PROBE_ORIGIN pointed at its own ingress because there
is no edge locally). It is `--profile extras`, so a default `docker compose up` is unchanged.

title: [tunnel-protocol] 4.2 Integration Implementation
description:
Wire up the integration points and make the integration tests pass. Notes: X/Y integration tests passing.

Repo: debugg-ai-mcp. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §3 (wire protocol). Arc epic: debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.1.
notes:
INTEGRATION IMPLEMENTATION DONE — the ws adapter, and the whole protocol suite green.

  `__tests__`/integration/tunnelProtocol.test.ts   Tests: 7 passed, 7 total
  `__tests__`/services/tunnel/protocol + the above: 236 passed, 236 total (6 suites)
  Under jest.integration.config.js with --detectOpenHandles: 7 passed, no open
  handles, jest exits on its own.
  200 concurrent streams carrying about 13 MB each way now complete in 123 ms.

WHAT WAS BUILT
services/tunnel/protocol/transport.ts — webSocketTransport(ws):
  - normalises ws's three inbound shapes (Buffer, ArrayBuffer, Buffer[] for a
    fragmented message) to a Uint8Array;
  - a text message is onInvalidMessage, i.e. session-fatal, per the spec;
  - reports the socket's death EXACTLY ONCE however it dies: ws emits 'error'
    then 'close' for a live socket, so the error is held and folded into the
    close report, and a close with no code becomes 1006;
  - send() maps ws's send callback onto the session's un-acked-bytes bound.
It touches the ws types only structurally (WebSocketLike), so the protocol
directory still compiles with no `ws` and no @types/ws present — which is what
keeps it vendorable into the tunnel server.

THE BUG THIS PHASE EXISTED TO CATCH — a real deadlock, found only over a real socket

Six of the seven integration tests passed immediately. "200 concurrent streams"
hung: 19 of 20 streams finished in a reduced harness and the ONE stream bigger
than a window stalled forever, with both sides showing sendWindow=0,
receiveAllowance=0, unannounced=0 and an empty readable buffer.

Cause: node's flowing mode. `Readable.push()` hands a chunk STRAIGHT to the
'data' listener when the stream is flowing and its buffer is empty — the bytes
never enter the buffer and never pass through read(). The first implementation
counted consumption as "the length of what read() returned", so every byte
delivered that way was invisible, no WINDOW was ever returned, and everything
past the first 256 KiB stalled. Two sessions echoing 1 MiB deadlocked on it.

Fix (stream.ts): consumption is now measured as a DIFFERENCE, `pushedTotal -
readableLength`, reconciled on every read() and immediately after every push.
Difference-based accounting cannot miss a delivery path, whichever way node
chooses to hand the bytes over. Inbound bytes go through deliver() / deliverEnd()
now; nothing calls push() directly.

REGRESSION TEST, verified to actually catch it:
"transfers larger than one window > keeps flowing past the first window when the
consumer is a data listener" — 4 MiB (sixteen windows) between two sessions with
a 'data' listener. Restoring the original increment-based read() accounting makes
it fail on a timeout; with the fix it passes in 17 ms. My first attempt at this
test did NOT reproduce the bug (node's maybeReadMore calls read(0), and
difference-based accounting reconciles there, so only the original increment
logic shows it) — so the test was rewritten until reverting the fix actually
turned it red.

This is the clearest argument in the arc for having an integration phase at all:
the unit suite was 225 tests green with a deadlock sitting in the middle of the
flow-control implementation.
close_reason: ws adapter implemented; all 7 integration tests green (200 streams, ~13MB each way, in 123ms) and 236 protocol tests total. Found and fixed a real deadlock the 225 green unit tests had missed: node's flowing mode bypasses read(), so consumption accounting missed every byte delivered straight to a 'data' listener and credit was never returned. Consumption is now difference-based; regression test verified to fail without the fix.

title: [tunnel-protocol] 2.2 Write Failing Integration Tests
description:
Write integration tests for the paths that cross boundaries. Confirm they fail. Record the count in notes.

Arc specifics:
- two endpoints over a real `ws` loopback server: 200 concurrent streams of random sizes arrive byte-exact
- slow consumer: memory stays bounded end to end (backpressure works across the socket)
- abrupt socket close: every open stream errors; nothing hangs

Repo: debugg-ai-mcp. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §3 (wire protocol). Arc epic: debugg_ai_mcp-xkoh.1.
notes:
FAILING INTEGRATION TESTS WRITTEN (red, for the right reason)

File: `__tests__/integration/tunnelProtocol.test.ts` — 7 tests, all red.
Dependency added for it: `ws` ^8.21.3 (dependencies — the debugg transport needs
it at runtime) and `@types/ws` ^8.18.1 (devDependencies). Installed with
--ignore-scripts so the root `prepare` -> `npm run build` did not fire in a
worktree shared with the mcp-client agent.

RESULT
  node --experimental-vm-modules node_modules/jest/bin/jest.js `__tests__/integration/tunnelProtocol.test.ts`
  Test Suites: 1 failed, 1 total
  Tests:       7 failed, 7 total   (0.25 s)
All 7 fail inside the protocol stubs: buildHandshakeHeaders (handshake.ts:52) and
validateHandshakeRequest (handshake.ts:76), both `not implemented`. No timeouts,
no socket errors, nothing failing on the harness itself.

Full suite after this file: `npm test` -> Test Suites 14 failed, 72 passed, 1
skipped; Tests 312 failed, 1136 passed. The 14 are the 6 new protocol files
(5 unit + this one) and 8 belonging to the mcp-client arc. Every pre-existing
suite still passes.

WHAT IT COVERS (the bead's three, plus three the requirements imply)
1. 200 concurrent streams of assorted sizes (every 20th is 1 MiB, the rest
   1 B..32 KiB) over one real ws loopback socket, echoed back by the client the
   way the MCP will pipe to Caddy, compared by sha256 in both directions, and the
   stream count back to 0 on both sides afterwards.
2. Slow consumer: an 8 MiB lazy producer against a reader that takes 64 KiB every
   5 ms. Asserts every byte arrives AND that max(produced - consumed) stays under
   INITIAL_WINDOW + 2 MiB, i.e. what is in flight is a function of the window,
   not of how much there is to send.
3. Abrupt socket loss: 20 streams mid-transfer, ws.terminate(), then every stream
   on BOTH sides must error, both sessions must close and both stream counts must
   reach 0 — the "nothing hangs" half is enforced by bounded waits, not by the
   jest timeout.
4. The real upgrade handshake: a 101 that echoes X-Debugg-Tunnel-Protocol, and an
   unsupported version that comes back as a 426 with X-Debugg-Tunnel-Supported
   through ws's 'unexpected-response' path. This is the one piece of the protocol
   that only exists at the HTTP layer, so a unit test cannot prove it.
5. GOAWAY over a real socket: the in-flight stream still completes, then the
   socket closes 1000.
6. A control-channel PROBE answered by the server's onProbe handler.

HARNESS NOTES FOR THE SERVER ARC (xkoh.3): startTunnelServer() in this file is
the shape a real tunnel server's upgrade path takes — validateHandshakeRequest in
the http 'upgrade' handler, a hand-written HTTP response for a rejection,
wss.handleUpgrade + webSocketTransport for an accept, and a 'headers' listener to
put the negotiated version on the 101. perMessageDeflate: false and
maxPayload: MAX_FRAME_SIZE are set on both the WebSocketServer and the client,
per the spec.

TEST-HYGIENE NOTES
- This file is picked up by BOTH `npm test` and `npm run test:integration`
  (jest.config.js's testRegex matches any *.test.ts). The integration config has
  no forceExit, so every ws, WebSocketServer and http.Server is registered in a
  cleanup stack and torn down in afterEach. Verified with --detectOpenHandles
  under jest.integration.config.js: no open handles, jest exits on its own.
- It needs no binary and no network, so unlike `__tests__/integration/caddyProxy.`
  test.ts it never self-skips.
- Every test carries an explicit 30 s timeout, because under the DEFAULT config
  the timeout is 5 s, not the integration config's 90 s.
- The harness catches anything thrown in the upgrade handler and rethrows it at
  the waiting client. Without that, a throw inside the handler left the client
  socket hanging and the suite took 35 s to report the wrong thing; with it the
  same run takes 0.25 s and names the stub.
- Type checked with a standalone tsconfig (the repo tsconfig excludes `__tests__`
  and ts-jest is transpile-only): clean.
close_reason: 7 integration tests over a real ws loopback (200 concurrent streams byte-exact, slow-consumer memory bound, abrupt socket loss, the real 101/426 handshake, GOAWAY drain, PROBE). All red inside the handshake stubs, no timeouts, suite runs in 0.25s and leaks no handles. ws + @types/ws added to package.json.

title: Agent cannot reliably OPEN a custom dropdown/listbox (run 1 of az1p)
description:
Split out of debugg_ai_mcp-az1p. That bead carried TWO defects; the ENUMERATION half
(open list, options below the fold) is fixed by the read_options action. This is the
other half and is untouched by it.

REPRO (execution df973e60-cec3-4fce-bac7-407e3d6869ad, 2026-08-02): the agent clicked
the trigger of a real 9-option dropdown and reported it could not open the list.
-> fail: "the dropdown list is not open, so the option labels ... cannot be verified"

This is an INTERACTION failure, not a perception one. Candidate causes, none confirmed:
- the click lands on a wrapper rather than the trigger (Radix/shadcn triggers nest a
  span + an icon inside the button);
- the control opens on keydown (Enter / Space / Alt+ArrowDown) rather than on a
  synthetic click;
- the popover opens and closes again before the next observation (focus/blur race);
- the click misses because the element moved between the DOM snapshot and the click.

NOTE the diagnostics are now better than they were: read_options on a page with nothing
open returns an explicit "no option list is present ... the control did not open", so a
run in this state should now SAY that rather than guess. That is a better report, not a
fix — the agent still cannot open the control.

FIRST STEP: re-read df973e60's step records for what the click actually targeted, and
check whether a keyboard fallback (focus + Enter / Alt+ArrowDown) opens the same control.

title: check_app_in_browser ignores a supplied ?query deep link (re-navigates instead), and a multi-level drill exhausts the 600s budget
description:
check_app_in_browser cannot verify anything that is only reachable via a deep link
or behind several drill-downs — two independent limits, both hit on one task.

OBSERVED 2026-08-02 while verifying a state-level dock on the validation canvas
(four separate runs):

 1. THE DEEP LINK IS NOT PRESERVED. The task URL carried `?node=<id>`, which the app
    uses to restore a selected node and open its detail panel. The agent did not land
    on it — it re-navigated to the section from the sidebar, losing the query entirely.
    The app's own URL contract (ref/env/node are mirrored so a back-nav restores the
    view) is therefore unusable as a verification entry point, and the only remaining
    route to that state is manual drilling.
 2. MANUAL DRILLING EXCEEDS THE BUDGET. Reaching the same state by hand is a 3-level
    section drill, which exceeded the 600s per-call limit.

So a state that IS reachable and IS rendering correctly could not be gated. The agent
verified the surrounding surface (canvas, rails, coverage pill) and said plainly that
the state-level check did not complete — the right call, but the check is exactly the
one that mattered.

WHY THE DEEP LINK MATTERS MORE THAN THE BUDGET: passing a URL is the cheapest, most
deterministic way to put the browser in a specific state, and it is how a caller
avoids spending steps on navigation. If the agent silently re-navigates instead of
honouring the URL it was given, every deep-link verification is quietly testing
something else. Compare `debugg_ai_mcp-go1m`, where `auth.deepUrl` is also not
honoured — the same class: URLs the caller supplies are not treated as authoritative.

FIX DIRECTION:
 1. Land on the EXACT url given, query string included, and do not re-navigate away
    from it unless the task says to. If a redirect moves it, report that as a finding
    rather than silently continuing.
 2. Report budget exhaustion as `inconclusive`, not `fail` (see debugg_ai_mcp-0cyr) —
    "I ran out of steps" is not "the app is broken".
 3. Consider a `steps`/`timeout` override for tasks the caller knows are deep, or a
    documented "put the browser here, then assert" mode that spends no agent budget on
    navigation.

Evidence: four runs on the wevug.2.6 verification; details on that bead. The state in
question was subsequently confirmed correct by other means (real logged-in Chromium),
so this is purely a tooling gap, not a product defect.

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text:
PARTIAL (query-preservation half), 2026-08-02 — filed from the go1m fix.

The 'supplied URLs are not authoritative' class is now closed on the MCP side for
every URL the MCP forwards: retargetAuxiliaryUrl (utils/tunnelContext.ts) rewrites
via retargetTunnelUrl, which preserves pathname + search + hash. Regression test
asserts a supplied ?env=env:abc&node=n-42&foo=bar#panel survives the rewrite with
every param intact — the test this bead asked for.

STILL OPEN, and it is the part that matters here: the MCP was never dropping the
?query. It forwards contextData.targetUrl with the query attached. The re-navigation
described in this bead ('the agent re-navigated to the section from the sidebar,
losing the query entirely') is BROWSER-AGENT behaviour, platform-side — the agent
chooses to navigate rather than honouring the URL it was handed. So fix direction
#1 ('land on the EXACT url given ... do not re-navigate away from it unless the
task says to') belongs in sentinal, not here, and needs a bead there.

Fix direction #2 ('report budget exhaustion as inconclusive, not fail') is the
same routing problem as 0cyr/6b4a/az1p — see the note on 0cyr. Worth knowing: the
contract enum ALREADY has the vocabulary (pass|fail|inconclusive|error|timeout,
serializers.py:1149) and _derive_contract_verdict ALREADY routes an exhausted step
budget to 'timeout' (:740, via state['budget_exhausted']). So for the 600s wall
clock the remaining work is making the 600s timeout set that flag, not inventing
an outcome.

title: No scroll-within-element action: options below the fold in an open listbox are unverifiable, and the run grades 'fail'
description:
The agent cannot scroll INSIDE an open listbox/popover, so any control with more
options than fit is unverifiable — and the run grades `fail` for it.

REPRODUCED 2026-08-02, twice, on a real dropdown with 9 options:
  run 1: clicked the trigger; reported it could not open the list.
          -> fail: "the dropdown list is not open, so the option labels ... cannot
             be verified"
  run 2: opened it, then issued `scroll_down_0.7_pages` — which scrolled the PAGE,
          not the listbox, so the lower options stayed clipped.
          -> fail: "the dropdown is open, but the screenshots only show a partial
             list of options, with the lower items cut off/scrollable; the exact
             full set of option labels cannot be determined"

The honesty is right — it refused to claim what it could not see, which is the
behaviour we want. The defect is the missing CAPABILITY behind it: there is no
scroll-within-element action, so a scrollable popover is a blind spot. The full list
WAS visible in the returned screenshot, so the information reached the caller; only
the agent's own enumeration failed.

WHY IT MATTERS: "enumerate the options in this control and check none are
duplicated" is a core visual-QA task, and it is exactly the kind of check a human
would delegate. Menus, comboboxes, long select lists, virtualised tables and any
`overflow:auto` panel are all affected.

FIX DIRECTION, roughly in order of value:
 1. a scroll action scoped to an ELEMENT (scroll the nearest scrollable ancestor of
    a target), not just the page;
 2. read option text from the accessibility tree / DOM rather than from pixels — a
    `role=listbox`'s `option` children are enumerable without scrolling at all, and
    that removes the whole class for menus and selects;
 3. failing both, grade this `inconclusive` rather than `fail`, per
    debugg_ai_mcp-0cyr — "I could not see all of it" is not "the app is broken".

Evidence: executions df973e60-cec3-4fce-bac7-407e3d6869ad and
fc8cdac9-cdc7-478f-822a-d946ca6a7ebf.

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text:
TRIAGE 2026-08-02, from working x9hv/Theme 1.

CONFIRMED THE CAPABILITY GAP AT THE SOURCE. There is no scroll action of any kind
in the brains layer: grep for 'scroll_down|scroll_to_text|def scroll' across
backend/brains/ returns NOTHING. So scroll_down_0.7_pages in the repro is coming
from browser_use's own built-in action set, which scrolls the PAGE. That matches
run 2's symptom exactly and means fix direction #1 (element-scoped scroll) is
net-new action surface on our controller, not a parameter change to something
that exists.

STRONGLY SECOND FIX DIRECTION #2 OVER #1. Reading option text from the
accessibility tree / DOM removes the whole class rather than one instance, and the
machinery is already there: hallucination_guard.py already walks the DOM including
shadow roots and iframes (:579-:623, querySelectorAll over 'text, tspan,
foreignObject, canvas[aria-label]' plus frame recursion). A role=listbox's option
children are enumerable with no scrolling at all, and it also fixes virtualised
lists, which #1 does NOT — a virtualised listbox has un-rendered options that no
amount of scrolling-then-screenshotting will enumerate correctly. #1 leaves that
silently wrong; #2 makes it right or makes it obviously unavailable.

FIX DIRECTION #3 IS NOW CHEAPER THAN IT LOOKS. 'inconclusive' already exists in
the authoritative outcome enum (serializers.py:1149) — see the note on 0cyr. And
this bead is the cleanest possible example of the distinction Theme 1 wants: the
agent's own words in run 2 ('the exact full set of option labels cannot be
determined') are LITERALLY the definition of inconclusive, and it graded fail. The
honesty the bead credits is real — the agent refused to claim what it could not
see. Grading that as a product failure is what trains callers to overrule the
verdict.

Worth noting for whoever picks this up: run 1 and run 2 are different defects
wearing one bead. Run 1 ('could not open the list') is an interaction failure; run
2 ('opened it, but cannot see all options') is the enumeration gap. #2 fixes run 2
and does nothing for run 1.

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text:
FIXED RUN 2 (the enumeration gap). Run 1 ("could not open the list") is untouched —
that is an interaction failure and needs its own bead.

WHAT SHIPPED — fix direction #2, read the options from the DOM.
  backend/backend/brains/providers/option_enumeration.py (new)
  read_options action registered in browser_use.py::_build_controller
  _append_option_enumeration_guidance() in the system prompt (both terminal modes)
  read_options mapped to action_type 'get_options' in browser_use_adapter.py
  backend/backend/brains/tests/test_option_enumeration_az1p.py (30 offline + 12 -m browser)

It answers with one of three verdicts, never a guess:
  COMPLETE   every option incl. the clipped ones. Clipping is a RENDERING fact,
             not a knowledge gap — calling it anything else rebuilds this bug.
  INCOMPLETE aria-setsize > rendered count. Names the number: "6 of 240, the other
             234 are not rendered anywhere". This is the case direction #1 gets
             SILENTLY WRONG.
  UNCERTAIN  virtualiser markers but no aria-setsize to size the list.
Walks main document + open shadow roots + same-origin iframes (the hallucination_guard
k8x1f.7 traversal). Reports duplicates, since "check none are duplicated" is the task
in this bead. Cross-origin frames are named as unreadable rather than skipped.

TWO CORRECTIONS TO MY OWN TRIAGE, both material.

1. AN ELEMENT-SCOPED SCROLL IS NOT NET-NEW. I said #1 was new action surface. It is
   not: browser_use 0.12.5's built-in `scroll` takes an `index` and dispatches
   ScrollEvent(node=node) — element-scoped (tools/service.py:1264-1330). The repro's
   `scroll_down_0.7_pages` is OUR OWN LABEL, built at browser_use_adapter.py:220 from
   down+pages, and that label DROPS the index. So the execution record cannot tell you
   whether the agent scoped the scroll or not. My "no scroll action in brains/" grep was
   right and the conclusion I drew from it was wrong.

2. THE REAL REASON THE AGENT REACHED FOR A PAGE SCROLL. browser_use ships
   `dropdown_options` ("Get all options from a native dropdown or ARIA menu") and
   registers it with an EMPTY DESCRIPTION STRING — @self.registry.action('',
   param_model=GetDropdownOptionsAction) at tools/service.py:1539. The description feeds
   both the prompt action list and the tool schema, so the model is shown the name and
   nothing else. It is also index-scoped and searches that element's own subtree to
   depth 4, so it cannot see a listbox PORTALLED to body level (Radix/MUI/Headless UI,
   i.e. most modern comboboxes), does not cross shadow/iframe boundaries, and has no way
   to say "240 exist, 6 are rendered". Ours is additive; the built-in is left registered.
   A test pins that our description never regresses to empty.

VERIFIED
  - 30 offline: docker exec sentinal_django python -m pytest
      backend/brains/tests/test_option_enumeration_az1p.py -q
  - 12 real-Chromium: docker exec c_browser bash -lc "cd /app && python -m pytest
      -m browser backend/brains/tests/test_option_enumeration_az1p.py -q --timeout=600"
    incl. the exact repro (9 options, ~120px popover, portalled out of the trigger's
    subtree, duplicate BELOW THE FOLD) -> all 9 + the duplicate, nothing scrolled.
  - Production path, real browser_use actor Page + real BrowserSession: PASS. This
    matters — the actor Page rewrites JS source before evaluating and returns a JSON
    STRING where Playwright returns a dict; both are silent-breakage surfaces.
  - Real registry dispatch: model-facing schema is exactly {label}; browser_session is
    injected, not exposed.
  - LIVE AGENT, real LLM, our controller + the app-eval prompt, against a virtualised
    240-option listbox: the model CALLED read_options and reported "only the rendered
    DOM entries ... it is virtualized, so the full set cannot be determined". Before
    this it would have answered "6 options" with total confidence — nothing on screen
    or in the serialized DOM contradicts that.

TWO FINDINGS FOR OTHER BEADS.

A. NEW EVIDENCE FOR DIRECTION #3, produced live. In that virtualised run browser_use's
   OWN judge graded the honest answer FAIL: "the agent ... explicitly stated the full
   set could not be determined, which is an accurate limitation report, but it is not
   task completion." So the fail-instead-of-inconclusive pressure is not only in our
   serializer — it is also in the library's judge, upstream of us. Worth knowing for
   0cyr / js8yn: adding _concurring_verdict does not reach this one.

B. THE CLIPPED CASE IS NOT ALWAYS BROKEN. On a live agent run against the plain
   9-option clipped fixture the model answered correctly WITHOUT calling read_options —
   browser_use's serialized page state already carried the off-screen option text
   (innerText includes overflow-clipped text). So the production repro's failure was
   probably not "the text was unavailable" but "the model distrusted the DOM text
   against the screenshot", or a DOM-state truncation on a much larger page. Someone
   re-reading df973e60/fc8cdac9 should check which — it changes what else is needed.

NOT VERIFIED: no wni_frontend live-stack run and no MCP check_app_in_browser run. Both
MCP servers point at PRODUCTION, which does not carry this change, so an MCP run would
have verified the deployed agent and not this one. Nothing here is user-visible UI.

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text: Split the interaction half out to debugg_ai_mcp-adqo (agent cannot reliably OPEN a custom dropdown). This bead now tracks the enumeration gap only, which is fixed.

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text:
CORRECTION to my 2026-08-02 triage comment — I got a load-bearing fact wrong.

I wrote: 'grep for scroll_down|scroll_to_text|def scroll across backend/brains/
returns NOTHING ... so fix direction #1 (element-scoped scroll) is net-new action
surface on our controller.' The grep was accurate; the INFERENCE was not. I
grepped OUR code and concluded the capability did not exist anywhere.

VERIFIED FALSE:
  docker exec c_browser python -c "from browser_use.tools.views import ScrollAction; print(list(ScrollAction.model_fields.keys()))"
  -> ['down', 'pages', 'index']
browser_use's built-in scroll ALREADY takes an element index and dispatches
ScrollEvent(node=node). Element-scoped scrolling is therefore NOT net-new — it
exists and is reachable today.

WHICH MAKES THE REPRO READ DIFFERENTLY, and this is the part that matters:
backend/brains/providers/browser_use_adapter.py:227 builds the action label as
  details['value'] = f"scroll_{direction}_{action_obj.pages}_pages"
— it DROPS action_obj.index. So 'scroll_down_0.7_pages' in the run-2 evidence is
OUR OWN LABEL, and it cannot tell you whether the agent scrolled the page or
scrolled an element. The bead reads that label as proof the agent scrolled the
page; it is not proof of either. Anyone re-reading executions df973e60 /
fc8cdac9 should not treat it as settled.

That label lossiness is its own small defect — an execution record that cannot
distinguish a page scroll from an element scroll makes exactly this class of bug
unfalsifiable from the trace. Worth fixing alongside.

The rest of my triage stands: direction #2 (enumerate from the DOM/a11y tree)
still beats #1, and for a reason #1 cannot fix — a VIRTUALISED listbox has
un-rendered options that no scroll will reveal. That is now demonstrated rather
than argued: a live agent run against a 240-option virtualised listbox reported
'it is virtualized, so the full set cannot be determined' instead of confidently
answering from the 6 rendered rows.

title: Browser agent builds an invalid CSS selector from templated routes ({uuid}, ':', '?') — run grades 'fail' for a tooling error
description:
The browser agent builds a CSS selector from a route string containing `{}` and the
query throws, failing the run for a tooling reason with no product meaning.

OBSERVED 2026-08-01: a run whose task text named the page
`/projects/{uuid}/settings` returned `outcome: fail` because the agent constructed a
selector from that literal. `{` and `}` are not valid in a CSS selector, so
`querySelector` raises `SyntaxError` and the step dies.

This is not exotic input — it is the NORMAL shape of every route in this product.
Atlas templates id-bearing path segments by design (`/projects/{uuid}/settings`,
`/projects/{uuid}/validation?env=env:{uuid}`), so any task that names a page by its
route carries braces. The same class covers `:`, `?`, `&`, `=` and `#`, all of which
appear in the routes above and all of which are selector metacharacters.

COST: the run is graded `fail`, which is indistinguishable at a glance from a real
product failure — a caller who trusts the verdict concludes their feature is broken.
It is also silent about the cause; the reason text describes the missing element,
not the invalid query.

FIX DIRECTION: (a) never interpolate free text into a selector — escape via
`CSS.escape()` or match on text content rather than building a selector; (b) if a
selector does fail to parse, surface it as a TOOLING error distinct from `fail`, so
it cannot be read as a product verdict. (b) matters independently of (a): the same
confusion arises from any malformed selector.

Related: debugg_ai_mcp-0cyr (verdicts that report tool-side conditions as product
failures). Same family — a caller cannot tell "the tool broke" from "the app broke".

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text:
TRIAGE 2026-08-02, from working x9hv/Theme 1.

SCOPE: this is platform-side (sentinal), not MCP. The selector is built and run
inside the browser agent. Note hallucination_guard.py already wraps EVERY
querySelectorAll in try/catch (:617, :620, :623 — 'try { matches =
root.querySelectorAll(sel); } catch (e) { matches = []; }'), so a malformed
selector there degrades to 'no match' rather than throwing. That means the
SyntaxError in this bead is coming from the agent's own action path, not the
guard's perception layer — worth pinning the exact call site before fixing, since
the two behave differently today.

ON FIX DIRECTION (b), which the bead rightly says matters independently of (a):
the routing target already exists. outcome is a single-source enum
pass|fail|inconclusive|error|timeout (serializers.py:1149) and 'error' is already
defined as a system fault. So 'surface it as a TOOLING error distinct from fail'
does not need a new outcome value — it needs the invalid-selector path to set the
error narrative instead of terminating as a failed run. Same routing gap as 0cyr,
az1p and zf4g's budget case; see the note on 0cyr for the full picture.

ON FIX DIRECTION (a): agreed it is not exotic input. Worth stating the general
rule in the fix — free text from a task string must never be interpolated into a
selector at all. CSS.escape() only helps if the text was meant to be an
identifier; '/projects/{uuid}/settings' is a ROUTE, so the correct handling is to
match on text content or URL, not to escape it into a selector. Escaping alone
would turn a SyntaxError into a silent zero-match, which is worse — it would grade
'fail' with an even more misleading reason.

The bead asked for a fixture route containing {uuid} and ':' driven end-to-end.
Concur, and note the routes in the repro also carry '?', '&', '=' and '#' — one
fixture covering all six metacharacters is cheap and would cover the whole class.

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text:
FIXED 2026-08-02 (platform-side, sentinal). Not committed — left in the sentinal working tree.

WHERE IT ACTUALLY THROWS (measured against a real Chromium + browser_use 0.12.5 in c_browser, not inferred):

  document.querySelectorAll('/projects/{uuid}/settings')
  -> SyntaxError: Failed to execute 'querySelectorAll' on 'Document': '...' is not a valid selector.

The throw is INSIDE the page, from browser_use's own DOM-query tools —
site-packages/browser_use/tools/service.py:193 (_FIND_ELEMENTS_JS_BODY, the 'find_elements' action) and :115 (_SEARCH_PAGE_JS_BODY, search_page's css_scope). Both catch it in JS and re-report it (service.py:1256 / :1220):
  return ActionResult(error=f'find_elements: {data["error"]}')

So it reaches the platform as a STEP ERROR, not an exception. The platform call site that turns that into a failed run is
  backend/brains/providers/browser_use.py:1715-1719 (pre-fix numbering)
    return Done(success=False, reason=f'Step error: {last_step_error}', ...)
because 'Invalid CSS selector' matches none of the retryable patterns at :1694. That Done then hits
  backend/workflows/node_executors/_brain_act_provider.py:414
    'outcome': 'pass' if success else 'fail'
which had NO route to 'error' at all. Hence outcome=fail for a query that never ran.

The triage was right on both counts: the guard's perception layer does NOT throw (hallucination_guard's _DEEP_ELEMENT_COUNT_JS try/catch degrades to 0 matches — measured, returns 0), and the routing target already existed and simply was not reachable from the provider path.

FIX (a) — a route is never used as a selector:
* NEW backend/brains/providers/selector_sanity.py — the ONE route-vs-selector decision. looks_like_route() is deliberately narrow (leading '/', a scheme://, or an UNQUOTED brace) so it cannot false-positive on '#last-value', '[data-id="{uuid}"]' or 'a[href="/x"]'.
* browser_use.py _install_selector_guard() wraps the registered find_elements/search_page actions in place (keeps their name/description/param model). A route-shaped selector returns a corrective RESULT — not an error — naming url_matches/text_visible, so the step is not a failure at all.
* hallucination_guard.validate_schema() rejects element_exists with a route at schema time (reason_code selector_is_route) and names the alternative. url_matches/text_visible with the SAME string still pass — the route is not the problem, using it as a SELECTOR is.
* A system-prompt block ('ROUTES ARE NOT SELECTORS') so the correction usually costs zero steps.
NOT CSS.escape(), per the triage. Proven in the fixture: CSS.escape() on the route parses fine and matches 0 elements — the worse outcome you predicted.

FIX (b) — a genuine parse failure routes to 'error':
* _DEEP_ELEMENT_COUNT_JS now reports a TOP-document parse failure via a sentinel instead of swallowing it, so _run_element_exists returns selector_invalid rather than 'matched 0 elements'.
* BrowserUseBrain._is_invalid_selector_error() classifies the real messages from all three engines (Blink, browser_use's wrapper, Playwright's parser). Bounded corrective retries (BROWSER_INVALID_SELECTOR_MAX_RETRIES, default 2) then Done(output={'tooling_fault': ...}).
* The hallucination guard marks _tooling_fault when it terminates on selector_is_route/selector_invalid.
* _brain_act_provider stamps output_data['error'], which is the EXISTING single-source key: NodeExecutor._set_outcome maps success=False + non-empty error -> 'error', and subworkflow.return reads it as errored. No new outcome value, exactly as triage said.
The reason text now NAMES the cause ('tooling fault (invalid_selector): ... is not a valid selector') instead of describing a missing element.

FIXTURE (the bead's explicit ask): backend/brains/tests/test_route_selector_real_6b4a.py — real headless Chromium serving a real page at
  http://fixture.debugg.test/projects/<uuid>/validation?env=env:<uuid>&tab=runs#summary
driven with the templated route /projects/{uuid}/validation?env=env:{uuid}&tab=runs#summary — ALL SIX metacharacters { } : ? & = # in ONE route. 9 tests: the SyntaxError itself, browser_use's tools reporting it, the guard refusing it without querying, url_matches passing on the same real page, the CSS.escape zero-match, the selector_invalid sentinel, the guard terminal marking the tooling fault, the real browser error graded 'error' end to end, and no regression on a real selector.

TESTS: 49 unit (backend/brains/tests/test_route_selector_guard_6b4a.py, test_tooling_error_routing_6b4a.py) + 9 live. Full backend/brains/tests: 374 passed, 1 skipped.

NOT VERIFIED: no full stack run through the real MCP check_app_in_browser with an LLM — the eval-app credential decrypts to an empty password, so any live scenario needing login fails for unrelated reasons. The chain from the real browser error to outcome='error' is proven deterministically instead (real browser -> real error string -> decide_next_action -> provider outcome -> _derive_contract_verdict).

FOLLOW-UP FILED in sentinal: sentinal-ctea3 — the DOM-derived half of the same defect family (surfers/control/affordances.py:300 builds '#'+id with no CSS escaping, and browser_sessions/interface/elements.py reads are unguarded, so a React useId id like ':r0:' raises out of sense.dom). That is the ':' metacharacter on a different trigger; escaping IS the right repair there, unlike here.

title: Post-run reclassifier should evict the tunnel it proves dead (restores self-healing)
description:
Follow-on to q9f6. handlers/testPageChangesHandler.ts ~737-767 reads ERR_NGROK_* markers out of the RUN'S OWN EVIDENCE — per bead 4bui the only live-confirmed source of these codes, and the only positive proof that the remote browser hit our error page DURING the run. It reclassifies the verdict but does NOT call markTunnelDead.

That is where eviction belongs. q9f6 correctly stopped the health probe from evicting (it cannot produce a code, and a dead endpoint is byte-identical to a transient flake through it), but that removed the last self-healing path for a genuinely dead endpoint. The reclassifier has what the probe lacks: positive, live-confirmed evidence. Evicting there is safe and restores self-healing without the coin flip.

Reuse disposeUnhealthyTunnel/isEndpointGone from utils/tunnelDisposition.ts so the allowlist stays in one place.

title: check_app_in_browser: intermittent CDP 4010 / BrowserUseBrain.initialize infra errors (client-reported, not investigated)
description:
Client report from the same session, explicitly deferred by the user when scoping the credential work: several runs failed with 'Failed to establish CDP connection to browser: received 4010' and 'BrowserUseBrain.initialize() must be called before decide_next_action()' (0 steps, no browser session). Looked like transient service instability rather than app faults.

Open question for whoever picks this up: does the MCP's transient-retry list (utils/transientErrors.ts, bead kbxy) already match these signatures? If not, adding them would convert a hard failure into a bounded retry. Not investigated — filed so it is not lost.

title: check_app_in_browser: read-only 'describe what you see' runs graded fail by a forced assertion
description:
CORRECTED after investigation of execution a53ccd67-322a-42dc-a1a4-cd10a42dfa4d (live, prod, 2026-07-27).

My original diagnosis (stale terminal_mode on the Brain row) was only half of it. The BrainFactory backfill was right and did help — it converted a false FAIL into an INCONCLUSIVE — but it does not close the complaint.

Actual mechanism, traced end to end:
1. In observe mode brain.act DOES emit outcome='pass' (_brain_act_provider.py:360).
2. derive_run_outcome erases it: outcomes.py:335, _OPTIMISTIC_DONE_MAX_STEPS=2. The run had stepsTaken=1, meaningful_action_count=0, verified_evidence_count=0 -> 'unknown'.
3. serializers._promote_contract_outcome finds no [assertion: ...] marker, no dissent -> 'inconclusive'.

Root cause: every downstream gate is keyed to artifacts that ONLY done_with_assertion writes (verified_assertions at browser_use.py:772, the [assertion: ...] marker at :781). Observe mode by construction never calls done_with_assertion, so g5r1b's and js8yn's escape hatches are both unreachable from it. The verdict pipeline is assert-shaped; observe mode has no path to 'pass'.

Smoking gun: execution a53ccd67 carries a judge RunVerdict {passed: true, confidence: 0.99, authority: advisory} from a VISION-equipped judge that correctly read the screenshot. The serializer has _dissenting_verdict (passed is False) and _indeterminate_verdict (passed is None) but NO _concurring_verdict, so a judge that AFFIRMS is read and discarded.

BACKEND FIX belongs to the existing OPEN bead sentinal-js8yn ('check_app_in_browser verdict stuck on inconclusive', open since 2026-07-14) — add _concurring_verdict to serializers._promote_contract_outcome, ordered after the matched-assertion check and before _indeterminate_verdict, gated on a confidence threshold HIGHER than dissent's 0.5 (a wrong upgrade hides a real failure). Not a fabricated pass: _TRUSTWORTHY_DISSENT_SOURCES already excludes the brain's own narrative, and an independent vision judge is not the agent grading its own homework.

MCP SIDE: fixed here. The handler was rebuilding evaluation{} from raw subworkflow node output instead of relaying finalExecution.evaluation, reintroducing the self-contradicting payload that sentinal-sk5sl.1 closed (headline 'inconclusive' vs evaluation.outcome 'unknown') and turning passed:null into passed:false. Now relays; node-derived shape kept only as the pre-contract fallback. 3 tests added.
notes:
FIELD EVIDENCE — this fired FOUR times in one day (2026-08-01/02) across five agents doing product QA, and it is the single most common way the tool misleads a caller. All four were read-only 'describe/report what you see' tasks graded fail while the screenshot showed the app working:

1. 'FORM chip + Form badge both present' — described correctly, graded fail.
2. State-detail dock rendered its unverified state one-for-one with the payload; graded fail on an incidental 'hasn't been crawled yet' banner elsewhere on screen.
3. Dropdown enumeration: 'the list is not open' -> fail (see debugg_ai_mcp-az1p).
4. Same, partial list -> fail.
Plus historically: 'Debugger' in <title> read as an error banner.

CONSEQUENCE: I now instruct every agent to OVERRULE the binary verdict and judge on the screenshot. That is the wrong equilibrium — it trains callers to ignore the field that exists to be trusted, and it is dangerous, because...

...THE GUARD IS SOMETIMES RIGHT, AND THAT IS THE HARD PART. In one run the SAME mechanism returned text_not_found for an element the agent believed it had shipped — and it was correct: 20 green jest tests were passing against a component that was NOT in the live DOM. The browser was the only thing that caught it. So a fix must NOT blanket-suppress assertion failures on read-only tasks.

THE DISTINCTION TO ENCODE: fail the run when the agent's own CLAIM is contradicted by the page (it said X is present, X is absent). Do not fail the run when the task never asked for an assertion at all ('describe what you see', 'report the labels'). Those should grade pass-with-observations, or 'inconclusive' when the agent could not see enough — never 'fail', which reads as a product verdict.

A caller cannot currently tell these apart from the outcome field, only by reading reason text and the screenshot. That is the bug.

comments.author: Quinn
comments.text:
TRIAGE 2026-08-02, from working x9hv. Three findings that change the shape of this bead.

1. THE ENUM ALREADY HAS THE VOCABULARY. The contract outcome is the authoritative
single-source enum pass|fail|inconclusive|error|timeout (serializers.py:1149), and
_derive_contract_verdict ALREADY routes: exhausted step budget -> 'timeout' (:740),
derived error narrative -> 'error' (:741), no derived pass/fail on a FAILED
execution -> 'error' (:743). So Theme 1 is a ROUTING problem inside an existing
taxonomy, not a schema redesign. Nothing new has to be invented for 'the tool
broke' — 'error' is already there and sentinal's own CLAUDE.md already reads
outcome='error' as 'system bug requiring immediate fix', which is exactly right.
What is missing is that tool-side terminations do not USE those routes; they fall
through to 'fail'.

2. x9hv IS NOT SUBSUMED BY THIS BEAD, AND THE REVERSE IS ALSO FALSE. Confirmed by
running the real guard code against the filed repro. The x9hv rejection happens in
validate_keyword_overlap, which runs at browser_use.py:791 — BEFORE run_assertion
at :815. The guard rejected the assertion for not matching the GOAL before it ever
asked the PAGE. That is upstream of everything this bead describes: no assertion
marker is ever written, so _promote_contract_outcome has nothing to promote and
the _concurring_verdict fix proposed here would not have helped that run. x9hv is
fixed independently (see that bead).

3. THE DISTINCTION THIS BEAD ASKS FOR IS NOW PARTLY ENCODED. done_with_observation
(new, browser_use.py) lets the agent say 'the page is not in the state the task
assumed, and here is what IS there', page-verified, and records it under
Done.output['observations'] separately from verified_assertions. A caller can now
tell an observation from a goal-achieved assertion structurally rather than by
reading reason prose. What is NOT yet done and still belongs here / on
sentinal-js8yn: _concurring_verdict, and routing guard-exhaustion to 'error'.

ON THAT LAST POINT — a caution I would not want lost. Guard exhaustion should NOT
be blanket-routed to 'error'. Split it by the reason code that caused it:
  keyword_overlap / schema_invalid / target_empty  -> tool-side  -> 'error'
  text_not_found / element_not_found               -> the page contradicted the
                                                      agent's claim -> 'fail'
That second row is the 20-green-jest-tests case. Routing all exhaustion to 'error'
would hide it, which is the exact regression this bead's own NOTES warn about.

title: [spike] Prototype: drive the intent-path workflow against a LOCAL Playwright (days-scale de-risk for m7un)
description: De-risking gate for epic debugg_ai_mcp-m7un before any production commitment. Prove the surfer+brain drive a LOCAL Chromium unchanged, using the ALREADY-EXISTING scaffolding: _create_local_session (browser_sessions/models/_managers.py:318-393), PlaywrightAdapter.from_browser (playwright_adapter.py:88-109), and the context.browser preset bypass (workflows/node_executors/browser.py:361-395). Target the INTENT-PATH crawl/E2E workflow (NOT check_app_in_browser, which rides browser_use and is out of scope for the spike). Success = the surfer's perceive/act runs against a locally-launched Playwright page with no browser-mgr allocation, producing a valid perception + at least one action. No cloud<->local transport, no browser_use migration — those are production concerns gated on this spike passing. Deliverable: a runnable harness + a go/no-go on the full build. Parent debugg_ai_mcp-m7un.

title: [epic] Local browser executor — kill the localhost-tunnel bug class by running the browser local + brain in cloud
description:
Direction for permanently killing the localhost-tunnel bug class: run a LIGHTWEIGHT browser
executor LOCALLY (Playwright in / driven by the MCP process, reaching localhost directly — no
tunnel), while the decision BRAIN + JUDGE stay in the cloud. Captured from a two-sided read-only
feasibility spike (2026-07-17). NOT scheduled — this is the big build; near-term we keep fixing
the existing ngrok tunnel (zmc9, k34o). File so the findings aren't lost.

## Why
Every localhost tunnel bug we fight (z15n, pqgj, k6yq, zmc9) exists only because the browser runs
in the cloud and the app is on localhost, so we punch an inbound ngrok tunnel. Move the browser to
the machine that can already reach localhost and the whole bug class disappears.

## Feasibility: YES, with one trap and one blocker

GOOD (both sides confirmed, file:line evidence in the spike transcripts):
- sentinal's `b_session` seam is genuinely transport-agnostic: surfer/brain drive a duck-typed
  `page: Any` with ZERO browser-mgr type leakage (grep-verified). A local Playwright is a drop-in
  second implementation. Pluggability 2/5. (browser_sessions/interface/{session,control,content,
  elements,waits,browser}.py; surfers/control/controller.py:231-252.)
- A local-Chromium path ALREADY half-exists and is used by eval harnesses: _create_local_session
  does chromium.launch() (browser_sessions/models/_managers.py:318-393); PlaywrightAdapter.from_browser
  (playwright_adapter.py:88-109); a context.browser preset bypass skips browser-mgr entirely
  (workflows/node_executors/browser.py:361-395).
- browser-mgr is ~85% multi-tenant farm, ~15% "drive a browser." Warm pool, container-per-session,
  Redis registry, TTL reaping, VNC, cross-worker recording — ALL droppable locally. Driving core is
  plain CDP (core/browser/cdp.py); Playwright is a strict superset. HAR/console/video are hand-built
  on CDP in browser-mgr and are FREE natively in Playwright. Only genuinely new work is UPLOADING
  finished artifacts to the cloud. Port only two things: --disable-blink-features=AutomationControlled
  and the GA/GTM host-blocking (compose/browser-session/entrypoint.sh).

THE TRAP (this is the crux — running local does NOT automatically remove a tunnel):
- If the CLOUD keeps the browser handle (holds the CDP/Playwright connection into the user-local
  browser), the cloud must reach INTO the laptop = a REVERSE TUNNEL, same bug class. WRONG.
- Tunnel-free requires the LAPTOP to dial OUT: run the browser AND the b_session/surfer control
  layer locally, ship perception DTOs UP and receive intents DOWN over the MCP's existing outbound
  connection. Only brain.think + judge stay cloud. sentinal already splits perceive/think/act into
  separate nodes exchanging serialized context (surfers/services/execution.py:616-674), so that cut
  line already exists.

THE BLOCKER (flagship tool is on the wrong path):
- check_app_in_browser does NOT ride the clean b_session seam. It uses the `browser_use` provider
  (workflows/factories.py:75-83 for_browser_use_evaluation; brains/providers/browser_use.py:248-274),
  a third-party agent that fuses perceive+think+act behind its OWN CDP handle — no think-boundary to
  cut. Corroborated independently by prod execution records (providerType=browser_use,
  brainName="Browser Use Evaluator Brain", brainId 985).
- So localizing the flagship needs EITHER migrating App Evaluation off browser_use onto sentinal's
  native intent path (which HAS the clean cut) OR running browser_use against a local Chromium —
  but the latter ships the LLM brain local (defeats the point) or reverse-tunnels. The migration is
  the honest prerequisite and the single biggest cost.

## Phased plan
- PROTOTYPE (days): drive the INTENT-PATH crawl/E2E workflow against a local Playwright via the
  existing local_playwright/preset bypass. Proves surfer+brain run a local browser unchanged. No
  transport, no browser_use, mostly existing code. This is the de-risking gate — do it before
  committing to anything below. (Tracked as a child of this epic.)
- PRODUCTION local check_app_in_browser (weeks–months): (1) migrate App Evaluation off browser_use
  onto the intent path; (2) build the outbound cloud↔local control channel (RemotePage-over-RPC, or
  local-node dispatch in the workflow engine); (3) rework session/recording/reconnect that assume a
  browser-mgr BrowserSession.

## Scope / non-goals
- Fixes the LOCALHOST case only. Deployed/preview-URL verification STAYS on the cloud farm — that's
  correct; the farm is what it's good at. This is specifically a localhost-inner-loop fix.
- Does not replace browser-mgr. Coexists: farm for deployed URLs, local executor for localhost.

## Caveat on confidence
Synthesis rests on the two spike agents' file:line findings (spot-checked, not re-read end to end),
except the browser_use blocker which is confirmed from two independent angles (spike + prod records).
The cloud↔local transport itself does not exist in code yet — the spike identified WHERE it plugs in,
not an existing implementation. A days-scale prototype is the right next evidence, not more analysis.

Related: debugg_ai_mcp-zmc9 (P0, current tunnel — stale path on reuse), debugg_ai_mcp-k34o
(tunnel-layer audit), debugg_ai_mcp-56kd (relay honestly epic).

title: probeTunnelHealth returns a FALSE NETWORK_ERROR ~1 in 5 runs (DNS race ~286ms after tunnel creation) — spurious TunnelTrafficBlocked on a healthy server
description:
Observed during live QA of e20e20a. The pre-flight tunnel health probe (handlers/testPageChangesHandler.ts:223-236, bead 1om) reports the tunnel as unhealthy on a server that is demonstrably serving:

    [warn] Tunnel health probe failed for https://<id>.ngrok.debugg.ai/: NETWORK_ERROR in 286ms
    >>> returned error: 'TunnelTrafficBlocked'
    $ curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' http://127.0.0.1:39117/   ->  200

Frequency: roughly 1 in 5 runs during the QA session. The ~286ms timing points at a DNS race — we
probe the freshly-created *.ngrok.debugg.ai hostname before it resolves, get a NETWORK_ERROR, and
report the user's dev server as unreachable when nothing is wrong.

## Impact (two ways, second is worse)

1. Directly: a spurious 'TunnelTrafficBlocked' failure telling the user their dev server is
   misconfigured when it is fine. Wasted debugging.
2. Via debugg_ai_mcp-4bui: the SAME probe is now also used post-run to reclassify a backend 'fail'
   as infrastructure. A flaky probe there silently converts a genuine UI failure into an
   infrastructure excuse. 4bui's fix (require the ERR_NGROK marker) removes that blast radius, but
   this probe is still wrong on its own terms for the pre-flight path.

## Suggested fix

Distinguish 'the name does not resolve yet' from 'traffic is blocked'. Options: retry the probe on
NETWORK_ERROR/DNS failure with a short backoff before declaring failure; wait for DNS resolution
after tunnel creation; or treat an unresolvable host within the first N ms as 'not ready' rather
than 'blocked'. A probe that cannot distinguish 'not ready yet' from 'broken' should not be
authoritative.

## TDD acceptance criteria

1. FAILING TEST FIRST: probe against a host that fails to resolve on first attempt then resolves
   -> asserts healthy (today it reports NETWORK_ERROR/unhealthy on the first miss).
2. Test: genuinely blocked traffic (resolves, but connection refused / 502 + ERR_NGROK marker)
   still reports unhealthy — no coverage regression, we must not paper over real faults.
3. Full suite green: npm test, npx tsc --noEmit, npm run lint, npm run build.
4. Live validation: run check_app_in_browser against a healthy throwaway server N>=10 times and
   assert zero spurious TunnelTrafficBlocked. The bug is a race — a single green run proves nothing.

Relates to debugg_ai_mcp-4bui, debugg_ai_mcp-z15n, debugg_ai_mcp-k34o (tunnel-layer audit).
notes: Closed 2026-07-15 — fixed in facf324, live-proven 0/12 spurious failures.

title: [bug] Localhost tunnel goes offline mid-session — check_app_in_browser lands on ERR_NGROK_3200 instead of the app, reported as a generic 'fail'
description:
A check_app_in_browser run against a healthy localhost dev server navigated to the ngrok endpoint and got ngrok's own error page:

    ERR_NGROK_3200
    The endpoint 687ba5fa-8dd5-45df-bfa2-32cdc09804f5.ngrok.debugg.ai is offline.

The local dev server was up and serving that exact route in ~57ms throughout. Adjacent runs in the same session, same URL, reached the app fine — so the tunnel was created, registered, handed to the browser, and was dead (or never came up) by the time the remote browser dereferenced it.

Two problems:
  1. The tunnel is not verified live before the browser is pointed at it.
  2. The failure surfaces as a normal task 'fail' whose reason blames the page ('The target ngrok endpoint is offline ... so the View button layout cannot be evaluated'). A dead tunnel is INFRASTRUCTURE, not a failed check. It should be a distinct, retryable error class — a caller must be able to tell 'your UI is broken' apart from 'our tunnel died'.

## Context
Hit once in ~6 attempts on 2026-07-14 while verifying a react-web-app UI change.

  executionId a8f07747-232f-4c37-87b5-9cf69f6e67ec — durationMs 217675, stepsTaken 7, failureCategory 'fail'
  browserSession 281b52fa-c0db-4705-a25c-63f5f3d4baec
  Dead endpoint: 687ba5fa-8dd5-45df-bfa2-32cdc09804f5.ngrok.debugg.ai
  Target: http://localhost:3011/projects/83fa71e2-ff6d-4cc3-9c19-272b024f08fa/graphs
  resolvedEnvironmentId: f9ee0391-b3da-4fc8-be38-4ba523d69483
  Server: debugg-ai-published (npx @latest)

The trace shows the agent waiting 5x on a loading page, then re-navigating (step 6) and finally landing on the ngrok error page (step 7) — so it burned ~3.5min before surfacing an infra fault it could have detected on the first navigation.

Local dev server was verified healthy immediately after: HTTP 200 in 0.057s on the same route, and its log showed the page's own API calls returning 200.

RELATED: debugg_ai_mcp-zmc9 (P0) — also a tunnel-registry correctness bug, but distinct: zmc9 is a live tunnel replaying a STALE PATH, this is a registered tunnel that is OFFLINE. Both point at the tunnel lifecycle/registry being trusted without verification; worth fixing together.
design:
1. Health-check the tunnel (cheap GET through the public URL) after creation and before handing it to the remote browser; fail fast with a distinct error if it doesn't answer.
  2. Give infra faults their own failureCategory (e.g. 'infrastructure'/'tunnel_offline') separate from 'fail', so automated callers don't record a UI regression that never happened.
  3. Detect ngrok's ERR_NGROK_* interstitial explicitly — it has a stable, recognizable body — and retry the tunnel rather than spending the step budget waiting on it.
  4. Consider auto-retrying tunnel creation once before the run starts; a 4-minute run lost to a dead tunnel is the expensive failure mode.
Relates to epic debugg_ai_mcp-56kd ('relay honestly') — calling a dead tunnel a failed UI check is the relay misattributing its own fault to the user's app.
notes:
=== BLOCKED by debugg_ai_mcp-4bui (2026-07-15) — do NOT close on e20e20a ===
The fix in e20e20a is HALF right.

LIVE-VALIDATED WORKING: a real mid-run tunnel death IS caught and correctly reclassified —
error='TunnelOfflineDuringRun', failureCategory='infrastructure', outcome='error', backendVerdict
preserved, ngrokErrorCode=ERR_NGROK_3200. This bead's open question is ANSWERED: a real mid-run
death DOES surface an ERR_NGROK_* marker in evidence.actionTrace, independently of the verdict
reason. Real code is ERR_NGROK_3200 (tunnel offline), not 8012 — killing the upstream drops the
endpoint rather than merely refusing connections. Both arms fired together (re-probe=NETWORK_ERROR,
marker=ERR_NGROK_3200).

BROKEN: the re-probe arm produces FALSE POSITIVES. Execution 2aa14b0b-3a30-48e2-a646-65357cf775e2

title: Architecture: stop destroying tunnels per-call for same localhost server
description:
Current pattern: every check_app_in_browser call creates a tunnel, uses it, destroys it in finally. For users testing the same local server repeatedly, this means:
  - New ngrok tunnel per call
  - New subdomain per call  
  - Backend has to reconnect each time
  - Race conditions during teardown/creation

The TunnelManager already has the infrastructure for reuse: findTunnelByPort() checks for existing tunnels and activeTunnels persists across calls. But releaseTunnel() in the handler's finally block defeats this.

Better pattern:
  - Keep the tunnel alive between calls (don't call releaseTunnel in finally)
  - Let the 55-min auto-shutoff timer handle cleanup
  - Only create a new tunnel if there isn't one for that port already
  - The tunnelId changes per call (it's the executionUuid) — decouple the tunnel ID from the execution ID for reuse

Note: this conflicts with the current backend expectation that the tunnel subdomain matches the executionUuid. Requires coordination with ai0/5vj work (dedicated tunnel endpoint). The dedicated tunnel endpoint returns a stable tunnelId that can be reused across executions.

Prerequisite: debugg-ai-mcp-ai0 (POST /api/v1/tunnels/), debugg-ai-mcp-5vj (pre-execute tunnel setup)
close_reason: Tunnels now reuse within-process via findExistingTunnel; revokeKey deferred to auto-shutoff; no per-call teardown

title: [bug] closed_at still NULL — normal client disconnect never reports closure
description:
Wiring CLOSED_URL (PR #588) was necessary but NOT sufficient. Verified after it deployed: closed_at is still NULL on 0-of-21 rows, including a fresh run that connected and disconnected cleanly.

ROOT CAUSE (read from the code, not inferred): reportClosed() has exactly ONE call site —
sessionSupervisor.ts:45, inside end(), which fires only when a tunnel is past maxExpiresAt (the 24h
cap) or when re-verify returns ok:false (revoked).

The NORMAL way a tunnel ends is the client disconnecting. That path is
controlServer.ts:231 — session.onClose(() => registry.remove(tunnelId, session)) — which removes it
from the in-memory map and reports nothing. So an ordinary close is never recorded, which is why
every row that was not explicitly revoked has closed_at NULL.

THE FIX NEEDS CARE, and this is the interesting part: on RECONNECT the server replaces the old
session with the new one, and the old session's close fires afterwards. Reporting 'closed' there
would mark a tunnel dead that is very much alive — worse than the current gap. tunnelRegistry.remove
already guards exactly this ('Only if it is still the registered one: a slow teardown of a replaced
session must not evict the session that replaced it'), so the correct fix is to report closure only
when remove() actually removed the LIVE session, and to make remove() say which case it took.

TEST IT AT THE RIGHT LEVEL. The test I shipped in #588 asserts the config invariant (every internal
route is wired) and passes — while the feature still does not work. That is the lesson: it tested
the wiring, not the behaviour. The test this needs is an integration test that connects a client,

title: [bug] tunnel closed_at is never set — CLOSED_URL not configured on the prod tunnel service
description:
Found reviewing 5 days of production usage (2026-09-25): closed_at is NULL on every Tunnel row ever created (16/16).

Both halves exist. The tunnel server has the caller (tunnel-server/src/verifyClient.ts:153 posts to options.closedUrl) and the backend has the route (tunnels/api/internal_urls.py exposes closed/ -> tunnel_closed). They were never wired: the prod tunnel service env has VERIFY_URL but no CLOSED_URL, and closedUrl is optional (readonly closedUrl?: string), so reportClosed silently no-ops.

Impact is observability only, not correctness or security: revoke works (revoked_at is set correctly on real runs) and the 24h cap still bounds a tunnel. What we lose is knowing when a tunnel ended naturally, so 'is this tunnel still open?' cannot be answered from the DB.

Fix: add CLOSED_URL=http://django.debuggai-api.local:8001/api/internal/tunnels/closed/ to the tunnel service env in deploy/prod/rc.yml, alongside VERIFY_URL. Then confirm closed_at populates on the next run.

Worth a test that fails when the two are not wired — an optional URL that silently disables a feature is exactly the shape of bug that shipped here twice already.
