title: resetNgrokModule() is a no-op — idle ngrok agents leak for days
description:
tunnelManager.ts:49-51, called at :322 and :587. Setting the local ngrokModule variable to null does NOT evict Node's ESM module cache, so the next await import('ngrok') returns the same instance with the same memoised processPromise and the same agent. The 'agent died, reset and retry' arm therefore does nothing to the agent, and nothing ever kills an agent that has no tunnels.

Live evidence 2026-07-27: five ngrok agents running, FOUR with zero tunnels, oldest ~5 days, all with live parents. Not tunnel-hour waste (no tunnels = no billing) but a real process/session leak, and it inflates the process count that gets misread as a tunnel problem.

title: probeTunnelHealth never yields an ngrokErrorCode on this edge — a dead port GOAWAYs instead of serving ngrok's 502 error page, so the NGROK_ERROR arm may be dead code
description:
Surfaced during the facf324 (pqgj/k6yq) work. PRE-EXISTING and unaffected by that change — filing so it is not lost.

utils/localReachability.ts:133-145 has an arm that reads ngrok's error page body, extracts an ERR_NGROK_* code via extractNgrokErrorCode(), and returns { healthy:false, code:'NGROK_ERROR', ngrokErrorCode }. Observed live: against a DEAD local port the ngrok edge does NOT serve that 502 interstitial to our probe — it sends an HTTP/2 GOAWAY instead. So the probe returns NETWORK_ERROR/UND_ERR_SOCKET and the NGROK_ERROR arm is never reached. On this edge, ngrokErrorCode may never be populated at all.

Consequences:
  - Any code branching on probe.ngrokErrorCode (rather than on the run's own evidence) may be dead.
  - The 'TunnelTrafficBlocked' pre-flight message says 'ngrok returned <code>' — a string we may be unable to produce.

NOT a correctness bug today: debugg_ai_mcp-4bui made post-run reclassification gate on the ERR_NGROK_* marker found in the RUN's evidence.actionTrace (which IS live-confirmed: ERR_NGROK_3200 when the endpoint drops, ERR_NGROK_8012 when the upstream refuses), not on the probe's ngrokErrorCode. So this is dead/unreachable code rather than a wrong answer. Health detection itself is fine and live-proven (dead port 3/3 unhealthy).

Hypothesis (UNVERIFIED): Node 26's undici negotiating HTTP/2 with the ngrok edge, which then GOAWAYs rather than proxying a 502 page. Could also be edge-version specific.

## Acceptance criteria
1. Determine empirically whether probeTunnelHealth can EVER return ngrokErrorCode against the current edge — try a dead port, a refusing upstream, and a dropped endpoint. Capture raw responses.
2. If it cannot: delete the NGROK_ERROR arm and fix the TunnelTrafficBlocked message so it stops promising a code it cannot produce. If it can: document which fault mode triggers it and add a test pinning that.
3. Do NOT touch 4bui's marker path — that reads run evidence, not the probe, and is live-validated in both directions.
4. Full suite green: npm test (baseline 844), npx tsc --noEmit, npm run lint, npm run build.

Relates to debugg_ai_mcp-4bui (closed), debugg_ai_mcp-k6yq (closed), debugg_ai_mcp-k34o (tunnel-layer audit).

title: ngrok.connect() fails with 'invalid tunnel configuration' on attempt 1/3 for EVERY run (4/4) — always recovers on retry, so it is pure latency we pay every time
description:
Observed on 4 of 4 live runs during e20e20a QA:

    ngrok.connect() failed (attempt 1/3), resetting agent: invalid tunnel configuration

It always recovered on the retry, so nothing user-visible fails — which is exactly why it has gone
unnoticed. But a 100% first-attempt failure rate is not a flake; it is a misconfiguration we retry
our way past on every single check_app_in_browser and probe_page call, paying the reset + retry
latency each time.

'invalid tunnel configuration' suggests we pass ngrok.connect() something it rejects on the first
call and that gets dropped/defaulted on the agent reset — i.e. the first attempt is systematically
malformed rather than unlucky.

## TDD acceptance criteria

1. Reproduce and capture the ACTUAL config object passed to ngrok.connect() on attempt 1 vs the
   attempt that succeeds. Diff them — that diff is the bug. Do not guess.
2. FAILING TEST FIRST asserting connect succeeds on the FIRST attempt with the config we build.
3. Fix the config; keep the retry ladder as a genuine safety net, not the happy path.
4. Live validation: N>=5 real runs with zero attempt-1 failures.
5. Full suite green: npm test, npx tsc --noEmit, npm run lint, npm run build.

Low user impact, so P3 — but it is a free latency win on the hottest path and a sign the tunnel
config is wrong. Relates to debugg_ai_mcp-k34o (tunnel-layer audit), debugg_ai_mcp-k6yq.
notes: FIXED in facf324, diagnosed from the real agent API (not guessed) and live-proven. ROOT CAUSE: getProcess() resolves at 'starting web service' (110ms) but the ngrok CLIENT SESSION is not established until 403ms — a ~293ms window we tunnelled into on 100% of runs. The resulting 503 ('a successful ngrok tunnel session has not yet been established', error_code 104) STILL REGISTERS the tunnel record; ngrok's own connectRetry pins opts.name on the first call and reuses it, so its retry collides with its own orphan -> 400 error_code 102 'invalid tunnel configuration', details: tunnel already exists. Our ladder then reset and reconnected with a FRESH name, which is the only reason attempt 3 worked. Captured config diff: attempts 1+2 share name=987be511-..., attempt 3 uses af6fb0ad-... — the name IS the diff. Also found: resetNgrokModule() was a NO-OP (Node's require cache preserves ngrok's state), so the 'reset' never reset anything; only the fresh name plus elapsed time mattered. FIX: new services/ngrok/ngrokAgentSession.ts starts the agent and waits for 'client session established' before anyone tunnels; ladder retained as a genuine safety net (tested). LIVE: attempt-1 failures 4/4 -> 0/12; tunnel setup 885ms -> ~250ms (~3x faster). Tests: reverting services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts fails 3 of 4 (independently verified). Extracting the module was load-bearing — an inline deep-require reached around Jest's ESM mock and spawned REAL ngrok agents in the unit suite (47 real failures); suite time 221s -> 11.5s. KNOWN GAP: startAgentSession's deep require of ngrok/src/process.js is unreachable by unit tests by design (covered only by the 12 live runs); ngrok is ^5.0.0-beta.2 so a minor bump could move that path — it then throws and falls back to the ladder (tested).

title: [FALSIFIED — see z15n] 'agent never types credentials' was really the tunnel failing to deliver JS chunks; app never boots
description:
When username/password are passed to check_app_in_browser and the target URL redirects to a login wall, the agent frequently sits on the login page issuing repeated no-op 'wait' actions until it hits a hard 'Node timed out after 120s' — never filling the form it was handed credentials for.

The credentials are valid and the app is healthy: the same URL + same credentials succeeded on other attempts in the same session, and a direct POST of those credentials to the login endpoint returns HTTP 200 with tokens.

Two distinct symptoms, possibly the same root cause:
  (a) Agent waits ~8 consecutive steps on a spinner/login page and gives up without acting.
  (b) Run dies at exactly 120s ('Node timed out after 120s') with ~250s total durationMs — i.e. the node timeout fires while the agent is still mid-deliberation, and the surrounding run keeps burning ~2 more minutes before returning.

Expected: if credentials are supplied and a login form is present, the agent should FILL AND SUBMIT it as its first action, not wait. Waiting on a login form can never resolve it.

## Context
Hit 3 times out of 6 attempts (~50% failure rate) while verifying a react-web-app UI change on 2026-07-14. Each failed attempt costs ~4 minutes of wall clock.

Failing executions (all 'Node timed out after 120s'):
  - aa9bef1b-1a37-4bdb-8b6e-9bc1aa147b4f — durationMs 253402, stepsTaken 10
  - c0295001-3cb1-463b-8053-eebff5352fcf — durationMs 253623, stepsTaken 11
  - 729a9d59-2018-4df6-87d0-a8011c2e482c — durationMs 253637, stepsTaken 10
  (note the near-identical ~253.6s durations — smells like a fixed retry/backoff ladder, not variance)

Succeeding executions on the SAME url+credentials: 8d308bd7 (85s), 0f09848c (63s).

An earlier trace (ad106bf1-a21c-4cb1-a5b3-9ff0cfdaaf2c) shows the pathology plainly: steps 1-8 are ALL actionType 'wait' with intents like 'the page still appears to be loading', then step 9 = done/failed. It never clicked or typed anything.

Target: http://localhost:3011/projects/83fa71e2-ff6d-4cc3-9c19-272b024f08fa/graphs (localhost tunnel)
resolvedEnvironmentId: f9ee0391-b3da-4fc8-be38-4ba523d69483
Server: debugg-ai-published (npx @latest).
Credentials passed explicitly via username/password params (the resolved environment has no stored credentials).

Confirmed NOT the app: dev server served that route in 57ms warm, and the server log shows the page's own API calls returning 200 during these runs.

One contributing factor worth checking — the app's login form is a CONTROLLED React form. Filling the inputs BEFORE hydration completes sets the DOM value but leaves React state empty, so submit silently no-ops with no visible error. A local Playwright script reproduced exactly that until a wait-for-hydration was added. If the agent types too eagerly it may be submitting an empty form and then waiting forever for a navigation that will never come.
design:
Investigate in this order:
  1. Does the agent have a 'credentials were supplied' signal at all? If so, make a login form a HARD trigger to fill+submit rather than something the LLM may choose to wait on.
  2. Cap consecutive no-op waits (e.g. 2), then force an action or fail fast with a useful reason. 8 waits in a row is never productive.
  3. Fix the 120s node timeout vs ~253s run duration mismatch — returning ~2min after the node already timed out wastes the caller's time and muddies the trace.
  4. After typing into a login form, verify the framework actually registered the value (re-read the input / wait for the submit button's enabled+loading state) before waiting on navigation — guards against the pre-hydration controlled-input trap above.
  5. Failure reason should say 'never attempted login despite supplied credentials', not the generic 'Node timed out after 120s'.

Fix likely lives server-side in the browser-agent loop rather than the MCP relay, but filing here as the user-facing surface. Relates to epic debugg_ai_mcp-56kd and to debugg_ai_mcp-56kd.3 (partial results on timeout) — a run that dies this way should still relay the partial trace + screenshot, which it does, but the reason string should be honest about WHY.
notes:
## FALSIFIED 2026-07-15 — I filed this bug. It does not exist. The real cause is z15n (tunnel).

Investigated with HAR evidence. The agent is not refusing to log in: **no login form is ever
rendered**. The tunnel fails to deliver Next.js dev-mode's ~47 JS chunks, React never boots, and the
page sits on the server-rendered 'Loading...' spinner. The agent's waits are CORRECT and its report
is ACCURATE.

The 'cleanest trace' I cited (ad106bf1) says the opposite of what I claimed:
  - 45/54 requests FAILED (status 0 / net::ERR_ABORTED, ~17s each), all _next/static/chunks/*.js
  - every one carried ngrok-error-code: ERR_NGROK_3004 (ngrok's error page returned instead of JS)
  - ZERO /api/ and ZERO /login requests in the entire HAR — there was no form to type into
  - it completed CLEANLY at 124.9s with all 5 nodes success — my 'Node timed out after 120s' and
    '~253.6s fixed retry ladder' claims were NOT reproducible on inspection

Measured on a healthy stack: 0/5 for the reported bug, 4/5 failures tunnel-caused. The
intermittency I attributed to a hydration race is TUNNEL HEALTH — runs reused the same dead host.

My proposed fixes were already-built features (verified in sentinal):
  - 'cap consecutive no-op waits' -> guard.py:128 already exists AND FIRED
    ('Repeated action (exact): 5 consecutive matching actions')
  - 'make credentials a hard trigger, not an LLM choice' -> _brain_act_provider.py
    login_precondition (bug y8ro) already runs the 3-tier resolver + deterministic
    fill_and_submit_login BEFORE the LLM decides. A clean-tunnel run proved it works.
  - the controlled-form hydration trap is real but belongs to a LOCAL direct-connection Playwright
    script (chunks load in ms). Over a tunnel React never even boots, so it cannot apply.

ACTION: fold into debugg_ai_mcp-z15n, which is the real bug and is genuinely this repo's
(services/ngrok/tunnelManager.ts). Keeping this at P3 purely as a signpost so the same symptom is
not re-diagnosed as a brain bug a third time. Sentinal counterpart sentinal-hwdie is likewise
marked NOT-A-BUG.

LESSON: this symptom has now been misdiagnosed twice from traces alone (once as a keyword
heuristic, once as an agent-behaviour bug). The HAR was decisive both times and should have been
the FIRST thing read.
close_reason: MIS-FILED — not this repo's bug; re-homed to sentinal-1e7wn. The relay owns none of this: 'Node timed out after 120s' matches none of the 5 transient patterns in utils/transientErrors.ts, so isTransientWorkflowError() returns false and the relay makes exactly ONE attempt. Corrections: (1) 'agent never types the credentials' is unsound — actionHistory records one representative action per STEP but maxActionsPerStep=10; the PASSING run 19d16ec5 logged in ('Login succeeded and the app shell is visible') with ZERO fill actions recorded, so absence of a fill in the trace proves nothing. (2) the ~253.6s 'fixed retry ladder' is the BACKEND re-running the brain node once at its 120s timeout — every error parent spawns exactly 2 brains ~2:01 apart (01:15:11+01:17:12, 01:38:16+01:40:17, 01:47:49+01:49:50) = 2x120s + overhead. (3) abandoned brains keep driving browsers ~8-11min after the parent returns (aa9bef1b returned 01:19:18; brains ran to 01:28:00/01:30:00) — backend cascade-cancel missing. See sentinal-1e7wn.

title: Caddy mode silent fallback — no user-visible signal
description:
When caddy binary is not installed, TunnelManager silently falls back to per-port tunnel mode. The user gets no indication that:
a) Multi-port support is unavailable (only one port per ngrok tunnel in fallback mode)
b) How to enable it (brew install caddy / apt install caddy)

Fix: when caddyAvailable is cached as false, emit a server-side log at WARN level AND surface it to the MCP caller via a progress notification message: 'Caddy not installed — using single-port tunnel mode. Install Caddy for multi-port support: brew install caddy'

This is a UX-only change, no API changes needed.

title: [chore] Back-fill DEBUGG_TUNNEL_* wording into existing company E2E brains and saved task descriptions
description: Found by the tokens arc (xkoh.2). New brain rows and task descriptions get the DEBUGG_TUNNEL_* marker wording, but company-scoped E2E brains and already-saved e2e task descriptions are one-time copies that still say 'ngrok or similar'. Harmless while both transports exist: the agent is told to fail on a tunnel error either way, and the marker text only sharpens it. Needs a data migration eventually, or it can age out as those rows are recreated. Decide after the rollout ramp (xkoh.6.2).

title: [tunnel-followup] Per-port hostnames: drop Caddy and PortLock from the MCP
description:
Put the port in the hostname (<id>-<port>.tunnel.debugg.ai, still a single wildcard label). The client then
dials that port directly, but only ports registered by in-flight tool calls. This removes the local Caddy
multiplexer, PortLock, the caddy-on-PATH requirement and the run_test_suite dedicated-tunnel exception.
Run it as its own feature-lifecycle arc. Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §7 follow-ups.

title: [tunnel-followup] Make tunnel URLs public
description:
When wanted: add *.tunnel.debugg.ai to the PUBLIC Route53 zone pointing at the public ALB, add the wildcard
cert to its listener (SNI), and route the public ALB to the nginx tunnel block. No code changes.
Design: debugg-ai-mcp/docs/debugg-tunnel-server-design-2026-09-19.md §4.
